Desktop, then the volume, is two clicks.

The same run photographs System 7's Standard File drawing `spinning brain ƒ`
(created from MacRoman bytes) — glyphs previously seen only on System 6.

**A coordinate harness has TWO assumptions about every dialog:** where the
items are, and what is in them. The first fails visibly; the second gives a
plausible frame of the wrong directory. ("Calibrated for System 6", 2026-08-24,
named the cheaper half.)

## 2026-08-25 (SuperDisk!'s second implementation) — the oracle was inside the corpus, and it runs on Linux

**Claim (measured).** Alysis's decoders run under `qemu-m68k` in milliseconds:
Disk Expander 1.2's `Cmpr` resources are one Add-In Module per codec, 68k with
no Toolbox calls, and `tools/sdmodule/` lifts all seven from a corpus fixture
and calls them. Every method 1..9 goes through two implementations in
`./ci.sh` — 4 corpus blocks, 14 from Alysis's 1991 compressor, synthetic blocks
for the six methods no reachable file uses.

**It found a defect at once:** method 9's Huffman region starts at the block's
LENGTH word, and the method is the low BYTE of the word above (the high byte is
that region's `startbits`); read as 16 bits a real block says 0x0809, so every
one was refused. BLOCKERS.md has the row and cost.

### Why this was reachable and nobody reached it

The modules were found 2026-08-22 and used as a table of names; nobody asked
whether they would RUN. They are position-independent, take a parameter block
in A0, and only "Tighter" calls back into its caller (a `jsr` through a
parameter-block field) — a thirty-line dispatcher. **A 68k reference is often a
subroutine, which needs a calling convention, not an emulated Macintosh.**

### What the harness cannot see, and why it says so out loud

Synthetic blocks come from THIS engine's reading (a flat 8-bit Huffman table
nothing real emits), so they grade framing, flag bitmap and context predictor,
not code assignment; agreement where both share a reading is not correctness.

**The one disagreement is named:** when a coded flag bitmap ends exactly on a
32-bit refill, the 1991 self-extractor and the 1992 module differ by one refill
on where literals begin. We follow 1991 (every reachable specimen's writer); the
harness counts those cases separately.

**Its "what would close this" was wrong:** four subjects sized so `ceil(ulen/8)`
is a multiple of four (`sdcompress.py --boundary`) were written as method 6 and
both readers decode all four. The real panel codes each flag in ONE bit, so a
byte count is no boundary. Still open: a real block measured to end on a 32-bit
refill.

## 2026-08-25 (SpaceSaver's INIT) — it installs, and it always did

**Claim (measured).** A boot of the installed image that never opens the
control panel leaves `System Folder:Preferences:SpaceSaver Preferences`
(`Pref/SMKR`, 10,496 B) on an image that had none, with and without the install
gate patched open. `INIT 0` runs — the opposite of what OPEN_ITEMS.md,
PROGRESS.md's M24 line and BLOCKERS.md had said since 2026-08-22.

### What the code says, which is what made the measurement worth taking

`~StuffIt SpaceSaver™` is a `cdev` with `INIT 0` and `INIT 1`; the install path
opens:

    2a50  link   a6,#-26
    2a5c  _GetKeys           ; the KeyMap at fp@(-22)
    2a66  _Button
    2a6a  bne.s  2a74        ; ...and 2a74 shows ICN# -4063 and RETURNS
    2a6c  btst   #0,fp@(-23) ; KeyMap byte 7 bit 0 = key code 56 = SHIFT
    2a72  beq.s  2a8c        ; not held -> on to the named checks

The mouse/Shift bypass is the ONLY silent refusal. Every other — no Gestalt
trap (`STR# 1001` #1), no `PERS` resource (#20), 'SLip' Gestalt already
registered (#8), locked volume (#9), full volume (#10), anything else (#3) —
ends at @0x2c8a in **`NMInstall`** with the message as `nmStr`, an alert once
the Finder is up. The twelve runs of 2026-08-22 all photographed a clean
desktop, so a named refusal never happened; `--patch-init` (that branch made a
BRA) behaved identically, preferences file included.

### The lesson, which is not about SpaceSaver

"Whether `INIT 0` installs at all" was carried three days and was answerable
from a 13,638-byte INIT and a `STR#` on the disk; the settling boot measured a
FILE, not a screenshot. **When a harness keeps returning "nothing happened",
ask what the software would have done if it had refused.**

Open then: the trigger — renamed `…small` subjects still came back
byte-identical; the preferences are written FRESH at every boot, so their
defaults (is the rule even enabled?) can be read off the image with `hcopy`.

## 2026-08-25 (SuperDisk! method 10) — a codec with no data, graded three ways

**Claim (measured).** SlowFastA is implemented and agrees with Alysis's own
decoder: 20 cases where the test encoder's input, our decode and the module's
decode are equal, incl. the wide-offset escape; in `ci.sh`.

Format: a 32-bit control word per 32 items, MSB first; set bit = literal byte,
clear = two-byte match (high nibble length, low twelve bits offset), copying
`nibble + 2` bytes from `out - offset + 1`; zero offset ends the block; a field
≥ 0xF00 escapes to a wider one.

### Why this was worth doing at all, when nothing writes method 10

"Could not be graded" stopped being true: the module runs on Linux
(`tools/sdmodule/`), so a transcription has an oracle whether or not any
archive uses the method. Of three unused codecs, 10's module runs end to end.

### The two things the oracle caught, both invisible without it

- **Match length is `nibble + 2`, not `2*(nibble+1)`:** one unconditional
  `MOVEB` at 0xfc, then a `DBF` targeting the SECOND move at 0xfe. Read as a
  pair, our decoder agreed with our encoder on every case and the module on
  none.
- **The wide offset is sixteen bits, not twenty:** `ASL.W #8` shifts the
  marker nibble out, so the escape joins the field's LOW byte with the next.
  Kept, the marker would put wide matches about a megabyte back.

**An encoder and decoder written from one reading agree by construction**;
three-way agreement fixes that, here for the price of a 302-byte resource in a
fixture already extracted.

## 2026-08-25 (SuperDisk! method 20) — the method that turned out to be an encoder

**Claim (measured).** There is no method 20 bitstream. Module 20 ("Tennessee")
answers `badCommandError` to decompress, compresses on command 2, and every
block it writes declares **method 11** — five inputs from 4 KB of zeros to
30 KB of text, each decoded back by this engine. Random data gets
`inadequateCompressionError`, as Alysis's published header specifies. Alysis's
own dispatcher hands method 9+ to the module of that number (INIT 32 @0x50c8),
which for 20 refuses.

### What the work produced instead

**A compressor for method 11**: the corpus has four SlowFastB blocks; now
`tools/sdmodule/` grades the decoder against any number Alysis's encoder makes.

### The shape of the mistake, which is the transferable part

"Methods 10, 13 and 20" are **module numbers** — codec identities, each
implementing compression, decompression or both (`thisModuleNumber`,
`compressAddress`, `decompressAddress` in Alysis's header). 20 and 13 compress
only: one codec with no data, one with no decoder to need, one implementable
all along. **Ask what a number identifies before asking why nothing uses it.**

## 2026-08-25 (ARC 0x0a and 0x0b) — the wrong attribution, and an oracle that was wrong

Both methods extract, graded against the CRC-16 their compressor wrote in 1988
and 1990.

### The search named a program that never wrote them

OPEN_ITEMS.md asked for "a `.arc` written by PKARC or PKPAK using method 0x0a
or 0x0b"; Crushed and Distilled are **PAK's** (NoGate Consulting; Distilled in
PAK v2.0, July 1989); PKARC's is method 9. The attribution sat in four files.
One search for the FORMAT found `ARC2PAK1.PAK` (three Crushed members, 1988)
and `IE111SEP.ZIP` → `INTRECHO.PAK` (ten Distilled), both named by the
ArchiveTeam wiki's PAK page, plain GETs from `cd.textfiles.com`. **A search
that names the wrong tool returns nothing for as long as anyone runs it, and
the nothing reads as scarcity.**

### The oracle was wrong, and only the archive's own CRC could say so

`unar` — primary oracle and `fmt_arc.c`'s transcription source — decodes
Distilled to the **right length and the wrong bytes** on 6 of 10 real members:
`XADARCDistillHandle.m` starts the 8 KB window at zero, PAK fills it with spaces
(as LZHUF.C), so back-reaching matches return NULs — text members fail,
binaries pass. deark, independent, agrees with the stored CRC on all 21
Distilled members in reach and is what the decoder follows and the suite grades
with. Upstream XADMaster is byte-identical to `reference/`, untouched since
2018.

Our usual ARC grading (generate, hand to `unar`) caught the crunch LSB-first bug
(2026-08-15) and would have failed here the other way. **When the reference and
the oracle are the same codebase, the format's own checksum is the only
independent party in the room.**

### The compressor still runs, and that is the corpus

**PAK 2.51 runs headless under DOSBox**, unpacked without root, `/CR` and `/O`
forcing Crushed and Distilled (`tools/pak.py`): seven generated archives reach
what the specimens do not — `pak-crushed-big.pak` alone fires Crushed's
table-full replacement scan **49,751 times** and inverted-literal mode
**13,009 times**; `pak-distilled-text.pak` plus the real archive cover all
seven offset tiers and 12 matches into the pre-filled window. PAK 2.51 also
expands its own distribution's nine members identically to this engine.

**"Nothing reachable writes it" is a claim about reach** — the third instance
in five days (DiskDoubler 3.7, 2026-08-20; SuperDisk!'s panel, 2026-08-22).
Ask first "what wrote it, and where does that program still run?"

### What was NOT done, and why

Method 0x0a also means ARC 7.x's Trimmed; decoded as Crushed, a Trimmed member
fails its CRC. deark's discriminator (PAK extended records vs ARC archive-info
items) was not implemented without a Trimmed specimen. (superseded: next
entry.)

## 2026-08-25 (ARC 7.x Trimmed) — the gap filed without looking, and the codec already in the tree

Method 0x0a's other meaning extracts too, hours later.

### The open item was a claim, and it had no evidence

"What is missing is a gradeable SPECIMEN" was filed the same session as the
withdrawn claim above, and nobody had searched. Two minutes: the ArchiveTeam
wiki links ARC+Plus 7.10 and 7.12; `ARC712.ZIP` is one GET and **the
distribution is the specimen** — four Trimmed members in its installer
archive, three more in the nested `ARCDOS.ARC` incl. `ARC.EXE`, the writer.
**A gaps file is not exempt from the evidence rule** ("I did not look" is not a
finding); BLOCKERS.md has the mechanism.

### The decoder was already here, twice over

Trimmed is LHarc's `-lh1-` (314-leaf adaptive Huffman, 64-entry distance code,
4 KB window) except: 0x100 is a stop code, so lengths run 3..59 not 3..60; and
the window starts as **zeros**, not XADMaster's preload. `src/unc_lzah.c`
gained a mode argument and nine lines; StuffIt method 5 and LZH `-lh1-` pass
`UNC_LZAH_LH1` untouched. **The second "new" codec in one day that was a
parameter on an old one** (Distilled: spaces; Trimmed: zeros) — deark's
`is_arc_trimmed` lh1 field said so. Ask what an unfamiliar method is a DIALECT
of.

### One method decides per ARCHIVE, and it is pushed rather than pulled

`arc_dialect()` walks the headers once and answers Crushed or Trimmed for the
file on deark's two signals; the result rides in the `method` int above the
header byte, so it survives the password path (up to four decodes per entry).
`unc_lzah.c` drives its own loop (shared with two formats), so this is
`fmt_arc.c`'s only PUSH path; rather than invert a decoder three formats use —
putting 930 fixtures at risk to save fifteen lines — RLE90 is written a second
time in push form.

### A copy with no decoder in it beats every oracle

`XARC.EXE` compressed with Trimmed in the distribution equals the
**uncompressed** 21,174-byte copy on another CD (`swsii/072/XARC.ZIP`) —
byte-identical, no implementation involved. Three of the archive's eight
members fail, **two of them STORED**, and deark fails the same three: that
`ARC712.EXE` copy is damaged. **When several entries fail at once, look for one
whose decoder does nothing.**

## 2026-08-25 (zip entry counts) — a count that wraps into success

A forum claim (no OS 9 application, not even StuffIt Expander 7.0.3, unpacks a
full `ftp.apple.com` mirror) prompted measuring our ceilings: four limits,
three harmless.

**The defect: a 70,000-entry zip listed and extracted 65,535 entries and exited
0** (`unzip` and CPython's `zipfile` say 70,000). The EOCD count is 16 bits and
the real count lives in a Zip64 record, so it **wraps into a smaller,
internally consistent archive** — 4,465 files missing, clean success. The other
limits fail loudly (past 4 GB `UNC_ERR_CORRUPT`; a tar member past 2 GB by an
explicit guard).

**Why nothing caught it:** the largest zip in 932 fixtures has **29 entries**,
and robustness variants perturb rather than grow. A harvested suite cannot fail
on a property no harvested file has.

**Two projects share the name "Zip64"; one was taken:** recovering a COUNT needs
no 64-bit arithmetic (total, directory size and offset read as two `uint32`s
each, the high half only compared with zero); addressing >4 GB files would put
64-bit offsets in `UncIO`, a libgcc call per operation on a 68000. A set high
half returns `UNC_ERR_UNSUPPORTED`; Zip64 proper stays out of scope
(OPEN_ITEMS.md, part 1).

**Not implemented:** XADMaster's kludge for writers exceeding 65,535 entries
without a Zip64 record (assume more if the directory has room) — a heuristic
about broken files with nothing to grade it.

**Ask of any width whether exceeding it yields an ERROR or a smaller valid
structure.** A COUNT that saturates agrees with everything downstream. Compact
Pro's 16-bit `nentries` IS that format's ceiling (no second record), so 65,535
is a limit of `.cpt`. Same shape as the gzip/.Z fallback NAME defect
(CLAUDE.md).

## 2026-08-25 (SpaceSaver's codecs, off the Macintosh) — the specimen problem, solved by the compressor

"Nothing reachable WRITES methods 1, 2, 3" (2026-08-22, the codecs) was about
the ENGINE's method choice, read as if about the codecs. **The `CMod` modules
compress as well as expand, and they run on Linux.** `tools/ssmodule/` is
`tools/sdmodule/` for a second format: modules lifted out and called under
`qemu-m68k` as specimen generator and second implementation. Every method
round-trips through Aladdin's code in **3 seconds**.

### What had to be read rather than guessed

- **The seven callback slots are NAMED by MacsBug symbols:** `ExpandFork`
  installs `cReadSource`, `cWriteDest`, `cGetSourceFPos`, `cSetSourceFPos`,
  `cGetSourceEOF`, `cProgress`, `cDebug` at +0..+24.
- **`cReadSource` takes its count by reference, `cWriteDest` by value** —
  reading both FSRead-shaped is the first crash.
- **Every vector takes two arguments**, the parameter block and the private
  block the module's `init` allocated (`LoadCompressors` @0x11a0 keeps one per
  module; `mExpandFile` @0x57e6 passes it); `CMod 10` reads five fields from
  it at once.
- **Alg 3 needs the preset dictionary too** (null pointer: fault; absent: wrong
  output). Methods 1 and 2 never touch it.

### Two properties of the "Original" modules, and why neither is patched over

- **Their store-this-block path is an F-line word:** `CMod 3` @0x5e4 and
  `CMod 4` @0x6ba execute `0xFFFF` on the give-up branch, reached by about a
  third of subjects. Nothing is emulated for it (that would invent a format
  detail); those runs are counted and every other fault fails. A hand-built
  stored block returned verbatim by both expanders gives the layout (flag byte
  1 at +0, big-endian payload length at +4, payload at +8).
- **`CMod 3` spins on a corrupted stream:** every module call needs a timeout,
  and our decoder must bound itself by the fork's declared length.

### The lesson, which is about the CONTROL and not about SpaceSaver

| picked | why it could never fail |
|---|---|
| the largest stream | that is the random subject — all literals, so it decodes identically with no dictionary at all |
| the best-compressing stream | that is 40,000 zeroes, which decode to zeroes however the stream is damaged |

Both printed passing controls. The control is now one deliberate file (ordinary
prose, no long runs), and neither check is trusted unless it compressed. **A
control chosen by an extremum chooses the degenerate case.**

## 2026-08-25 (SpaceSaver methods 1 and 2) — two codecs the day the specimens arrived

Methods 1 and 2 are implemented from `CMod 3` @0x634 and `CMod 4` @0x6e8, and
34 forks Aladdin's compressors wrote read back byte-exact (FORMATS.md has the
shapes) — the loop M32 built for SuperDisk!.

### The oracle finds what a reading cannot

Method 1 was right first time; method 2 wrong twice, neither visible in the
disassembly:

- **An unfilled table entry copies the module's copyright string:** the table
  is initialised to point at `CMod 4`'s last eighteen bytes, and five of eight
  subjects reach one.
- **A flag word of exactly `0x0001` looks exhausted:** the sentinel sits above
  the sixteen flag bits and is tested once per item at the loop head, never
  again after a reload. Testing again costs sixteen items, output staying
  correct until one is a match — 387 bytes of agreement before failing.

### How the second one was actually found

Table maintenance and hash were confirmed by direct probe (sixteen literals and
one match, all 4,096 codes swept through the module, agreeing everywhere).
**`qemu-m68k -one-insn-per-tb -d exec`** found it: log every executed
instruction, keep the literal-branch and match-branch PCs, diff against our
decoder's sequence — the first difference, event 290 of 306, named the bug. An
execution trace is a cheap oracle for "which branch did it take".

### The general shape, which is not about SpaceSaver

**A decoder that agrees for a while is not a decoder that agrees.** Both bugs
need an uncommon input; the sweep runs eleven subjects through every method in
three seconds — make specimens cheap, not precious.

## 2026-08-25 (SpaceSaver method 3) — the codec whose code assignment is a quicksort

Alg 3 is implemented; every SpaceSaver method decodes (FORMATS.md has the
shape).

### The code assignment is a sort, and the sort is not stable

`CMod 11` @0x27c assigns canonical codes in the order @0x15a's quicksort leaves
the lengths (Hoare partition on the first element, recursing into the smaller
half), so among equal lengths the code is a property of that partitioning.
**Any other implementation must reproduce the sort**; ours does iteratively
(no recursion, CLAUDE.md), smaller half on an explicit 32-entry stack. A stable
sort decodes most blocks correctly, since most have few ties.

### The tables are rules, not data

The module's init computes the length and distance bases (@0x1a04, @0x1aa0):
`extra[i] = i < 4 ? 0 : (i - 4) >> 2`, base 0 for lengths, the same shape from
1 for distances — checkable, and nothing new in `ss_dict.h`.

### The order that made it cheap

**Prototype in Python against the module, then port:** ten subjects
byte-identical before any C, and the C worked first run (method 2 took two bugs
and a trace). **When a reference can be RUN, the expensive step is the round
trip between a guess and a verdict.** Shorten that first.

## 2026-08-26 (an encrypted StuffIt 5 archive) — the pointer that was said not to work

**DropStuff 5.0.1 wrote three** encrypted StuffIt 5 archives on Mac OS 9.2, and
all three come back byte-exact (FORMATS.md, *StuffIt 5's RC4*) — closing the
item whose two "readings" were `unar` and our own generator.

### Position and click are different primitives, and conflating them cost the tier

The 2026-08-02 probe's five clicks all scored 0.0000 because the cursor was
pinned in a corner: the harness made an ABSOLUTE `usb-tablet` the active device
(Mac OS 9 has no driver), and a relative mouse saturates at ±63 px per ADB
packet. It never established it could POSITION before testing clicks.
**Establish the primitive one level down first**, on a target that MUST respond
(a modal alert's default button). Two of this run's click tests hit a menu bar
a modal suppressed — zeros meaning nothing.

### What defeats frame-differencing, and what beats it

The clock, a blinking caret and progress bars defeat diff-based cursor
location; masking pixels changed between idle frames fails because a caret's
phase aliases with any fixed interval. **Shape** works: the largest changed
blob (an arrow is ~100 pixels, a caret a sliver). Positioning costs ~40 s, more
than a sticky menu stays open, so menus are driven by Command keys.

### An application can refuse the FILE SYSTEM, not the OS version

Deluxe 5.0.1 (documented 7.5.3–8.5) installs on 9.2 but refuses at launch:
*"an update to this software is required for compatibility with the improved
Mac OS file system"* (pre-HFS+). **DropStuff, same installer and Engine, runs**,
so it wrote the specimens.

### A nag whose buttons move is an automation hazard, not an inconvenience

DropStuff's evaluation notice shuffles four buttons each time; a fixed "Not
Yet" eventually hits "Order Info", whose save dialog swallows the password
keystrokes (one cycle lost, looking like timing). The harness matches the
button's LABEL against a template.

## 2026-08-26 — base64 and MIME, and an oracle that is wrong three times

Asked for — and **already filed**: OPEN_ITEMS.md part 2's then-section 6 ("Not
implemented, and nothing blocks it" — emptied and deleted on 2026-08-26 when
its last entry, the disk images, was closed) had named it since 2026-08-25
(Macintosh Garden forum thread *Archive formats*), reference (deark's
`modules/xfer.c`) and grading already identified. **Cost:** an afternoon
re-deriving one paragraph, below a truncated grep, and one commit in which the
status file contradicted itself. The fourth growth of the brief on request
(after ARC and uuencode, SuperDisk!, btoa).

**Why it belongs:** base64 is what BinHex, uuencode and btoa became; a Mac file
mailed after ~1993 went as `multipart/appledouble` (an `application/applefile`
part with resource fork, real name and Finder info, then the data fork) — a
classic-Mac transport encoding with a resource fork.

**The reference:** mpack/munpack 1.6 (John G. Myers, CMU, 1994), whose tree
holds `macfile.c`, `macos.c`, `README.mac`. The CMU licence is permissive, so
unlike btoa (2026-08-23, *a reference that may not be transcribed*) it is
**transcribed** into `src/fmt_mime.c`: header rule, parameter parser, boundary
rule, `from64`, `fromqp`, filename lookup order.

### An explicit stack where the reference recurses

`handleMessage` → `handleMultipart` → `handleMessage`; the engine keeps a stack
of at most four boundaries and loops (parse headers, find the next boundary,
emit or skip, pop the levels it closed), scanning outermost-first as
`pendingboundary` does. The ~2 KB walker shares one heap block with its buffers
(`unc_mime_extract`); the chain the format adds is under 1 KB, measured with
`-fstack-usage` (FORMATS.md, *Stack*).

### The oracle is wrong in three places, and each one has a reproduction

1. **It never uses a `Content-Disposition` filename:** `getDispositionFilename`
   requires `';'` after the token `filename`, where the `'='` is, falls through
   and returns null; `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="b.bin"` is
   written as `part1`. We follow mpack's documented order (disposition, then
   `name`), RFC 2183's.
2. **It cannot read CRLF:** `ParseHeaders` ends headers on `"\n"`, so `"\r\n"`
   becomes the body's first two bytes, and `=\r\n` soft breaks decode as bad
   escapes, one invented byte per line (a text-mode reader). We handle both;
   the suite gives each implementation its form.
3. **It drops a decoded `\r`** (`fromqp`: `if (c != '\r')`), corrupting binary
   attachments with `=0D`. We keep it; `run_mime.py` asserts it on a subject
   munpack is not asked to grade.

"Graded by a second implementation" means *and the disagreements are
adjudicated*, not *and they matched*.

### deark and mpack disagree about a group that ends short, and deark is right

A base64 stream ending mid-group implies bytes (two characters one byte, three
two): deark writes them with a warning, mpack drops them ("Premature EOF").
deark followed. base64 has no length or checksum, so a message cut in half
decodes short and silently (as a uuencoded set missing its middle,
OPEN_ITEMS.md); the suite asserts that outcome.

### base64 unwraps as an envelope; MIME does not

`UNC_FORMAT_BASE64` joins MacBinary, BinHex, AppleSingle/Double, gzip and `.Z`
in both hosts' envelope lists; `UNC_FORMAT_MIME` does not, because the unwrapper
DELETES the consumed layer and a MIME part can carry a resource fork.

### The probe claims a message only when there is something to extract

Mail headers are no evidence (BinHex and uuencode postings have them). MIME
wants a `Content-Type` **and** a boundary, filename, or base64/QP encoding; both
new probes run LAST in `unc_sniff`, so a message with a `.hqx` body stays BinHex
(asserted in `run_mime.py`). Bare base64 is recognised by shape: four or more
full lines of one width between 40 and 76, alphabet-only, and a closing last
line — head AND tail. **0 false positives across all 940 fixture files**; diff
and robustness suites (932 fixtures, 9,320 variants) unchanged. A base64 file
too short to have a shape needs its `begin-base64` marker.

## 2026-08-26 (the btoa translator, by Apple event) — the door nobody tried

The btoa decoder had one encoder (`reference/btoa` 5.2.1). Aladdin's `btoa/atob
Translator` sat on the StuffIt Deluxe 3.5.1 image, unreached three times because
each attempt asked **how do I click that menu item?** — a hierarchical submenu
item, unselectable under Mini vMac.

### What the application says it will do is in its own resources

Read with `hcopy`, no emulator, ten minutes:

- `MENU` 132 (`Translate`) has two non-translator items; translator entries are
  built at RUNTIME from `Extensions:Aladdin:Translators`.
- The `aete` declares `translate` — `SIT!`/`TRAN`, direct object an alias,
  `trnm` the translator's name, `encd` the direction, `dest` the destination —
  beside `stuff`, `unstuff`, `segment`, `join`, `do script`.
- `SIZE` -1 is `0xd8e8`: isHighLevelEventAware **and** localAndRemoteHLEvents.
- Aladdin's `Translate Sample` script contains `.SIT!TRANnull … alis … trnm`.

**A route a harness cannot drive is not a route the application lacks**, and
the second list is written inside the application.

### Apple events need no scripting language

System 7.0.1 here has no AppleScript, and none is needed: `tools/aetran/` is a
~400-line Retro68 app that finds its folder via `GetProcessInformation`,
`LaunchApplication`s StuffIt Deluxe, sends `SIT!`/`TRAN`, and writes the reply's
`errn` to a file. One type-select and one ⌘O on screen.

### The dictionary says what the terms mean, not what the handler accepts

The first send, built as the `aete` describes, returned `-1700`
(`errAECoercionFail`). Six shapes sent in one boot: only `dest` as an `fss `
naming the not-yet-existing output FILE fails; an existing FOLDER, or no
destination, succeeds. `encd` defaults to DECODE (omitting it left a zero-byte
`Subject.dec`). **Send the matrix, not the guess**, when round trips are minutes
and the space is small.

### What the specimen was worth

The stream uses the older `xbtoa Begin` framing, MacBinary-wraps first, and is
byte-identical to `reference/btoa -o` **except the End line's `R` field width**
— eight hex digits vs this host's sixteen (`Crot` is a `long`, the reference's
rotate assumes 32 bits). Measured now, asserted narrow in `run_btoa.py`.

A real Mac btoa file is `X.MBin.ascii`, and `macextract x` stopped at the
MacBinary wrapper because btoa was not an envelope — open then, closed since,
btoa and uuencode both being envelopes now (2026-08-27).

## 2026-08-26 (disk images) — read the volume, not the extension

Seven extensions were asked for (`.dmg`, `.iso`, `.cdr`, `.toast`, `.img`,
`.smi`, `.cpgz`); six name a byte image of a volume, so the probe reads the
volume: an HFS MDB, an HFS+/HFSX header, an Apple Partition Map, and an ISO 9660
descriptor pair in any of four sector layouts (FORMATS.md, *Disk images*).

**All four came from `reference/deark`** (`hfs`, `apm`, `iso9660`), the ARC
oracle since M33 — "a reference this project does not yet have" was an
ungrepped directory, the second time this month. **The item reasoned backwards
about names:** `.cpgz` is gzip (already named), `.smi` is NDIF with no data-fork
signature, and the raw images are the ones with structure.

### What is corroborated, and what a 16-bit signature is worth

HFS wants an allocation block size that is a nonzero multiple of 512; APM a
map entry in sector 1 *and* 2; ISO 9660 a descriptor at sector 16 *and* 17 (as
deark's identify functions do). HFS+ has only `"H+"` in deark, and rule #1
forbids inventing offset 40, so it is corroborated by **the file being a whole
number of 512-byte sectors** — a claim about images, labelled ours in the source.

### The negative case has to be written the way the probe is entered

`run_diskimage.py`'s APM negative zeroed the block at 1024 — where the branch
*starts* — so a mutant without the sector-1 read passed. Zeroing 512 kills it;
all four corroborations were mutation-tested. **A negative test proves nothing
about a check the input never reaches.**

### The specimens were already on the machine

138 real images: Retro68's 800K test volumes, every emulator tier's disks up to
the 2 GB Mac OS 9 image, two 1.44 MB Garden floppies, a 224 MB Toast hybrid
(Apple-partitioned, not ISO 9660). Only ISO positives are generated
(`reference/pycdlib`, confirmed by deark and `lsar`).

### The tier figures were describing a smaller sample than the file held

A routine re-run returned **69/69** where every status file said 67/67: M33 and
M34 added two ARC fixtures to `sample.txt` on 2026-08-25 and ran only those.
Corrected in place (BLOCKERS.md tier table; FORMATS.md tier sections). **A sample
list is a number two places carry**; the sweep prints its denominator, so run the
whole list.

Compressed images stayed unnamed (the NDIF file opens into compressed data,
chunk map a `bcem` resource, fork not a whole number of sectors); the next entry
took disk images out of scope (OPEN_ITEMS.md, part 1).

## 2026-08-26 — a name is only worth something inside the frame the user came with

**Superseded for the Macintosh application 2026-10-18** (*the question after
the look*): it no longer names the format. **Superseded 2026-10-18** for
the engine and the CLI too: nothing is named that is not extracted (*the
formats it only named*).

The disk-image probe was removed the day after it shipped, and nine PC archive
formats named instead, from one observation: *a known format that is not
extracted is treated exactly like an unknown one.* Measured: on the Mac both
gave no output and *"This file could not be extracted."*; the unwrap chain breaks
the same way (`!unc_format_extractable(inner)`); the difference was one CLI line
and `UNC_ERR_UNSUPPORTED` vs `UNC_ERR_FORMAT` — 640 bytes of 68000 code.

**It stops being true in the user's frame:** opening an unarchiver says they
believe they have an archive; *"MacExtract cannot open RAR files"* sends them to
another program, *"not recognized"* to re-download. A disk image is not an
archive, so naming it changes nothing. **Detect-only is justified when the user
is already in the frame where the name is an instruction** — archives yes, disk
images no. Disk Copy 4.2 (detect-only since M9) went out the same day.

### Naming the archives is nine `if`s, and the references were already here

`reference/XADMaster` recognises RAR (three generations), 7-Zip, xz, bzip2,
Cabinet, Zoo, ARJ; `reference/deark` ar, cpio, Zoo, ARJ; every constant in
`src/fmt_foreign.c` cites its function. zstd, lzip, brotli, lrzip, WIM stayed
out with no reference in the tree (OPEN_ITEMS.md, part 2). bzip2, xz, 7z, cpio,
ar are written by their own tools and the suite requires **p7zip to open each**
before trusting the probe; Zoo, ARJ, Cabinet are hand-built headers deark must
identify; RAR and RAR 5 have no oracle in `ci.sh` and were measured once against
libarchive's test archives (decoded by our uuencode reader), as the docs say.

### The alert is what makes any of this real

The Mac shell had never named a detect-only file since M9; now photographed on
System 6.0.8: **"MacExtract cannot open RAR files."** Built from
`unc_format_name`; the longest name draws 46 characters against the ~60 the alert
wraps at.

**Moved, not deleted:** `attic/` keeps the disk-image probes, tests and suite
with a README (135 real images named, 0 false positives, four branches
mutation-tested); the change was whether they belonged in the product.
`UNC_FORMAT_DISKCOPY_RETIRED` stays in the public enum so no later enumerator
moves.

Everything a person reads became **MacExtract**: documents, the CLI
(`macextract`), the Finder name, the downloads (`dist/MacExtract.bin`,
`dist/MacExtract.dsk`), the alert strings.

**The `unc_*` / `UNC_*` / `Unc*` prefix deliberately did not change**, and not
for compatibility (nothing installs a header; anyone building on the engine has
vendored a pinned commit). **The prefix does not spell the old name** —
`unc_extract()` reads as "uncompress" or "unarchive" as readily — while renaming
meant 6,145 occurrences across every source file, 211 more in these documents
(many in dated entries, rewriting the record), and buried `git log -S`
archaeology. `libmacextract` in prose and `unc_extract()` in code are one
library.

**The header filename was the exception, and moved on 2026-08-26.**
`include/unclassic.h` → `macextract.h`, 26 lines; with no `__FILE__` or

**A rename can change a fixture:** `tools/synth_exo.py` fills its corpus with

**It found a variable with two spellings:** `tools/run_spacesaver.py` and

## 2026-08-26 (zip comments) — the second format with one, and the ceiling that moved

`fmt_exo.c` stepped over the EOCD comment (up to 65,535 bytes), excused as
*"usually boilerplate and `unar` does not write one out either"*;
`derived-MUSFMT10.ZIP` carries 495 bytes of author, address and format list
from 1994, written nowhere else.

**It leaves by Compact Pro's route** (2026-08-23, *Compact Pro comments*): the
`UncSink.comment` callback, the CLI's `<archive>.comment.txt` and `comment:`
line, the Mac's `Comments` document — no host change, the argument for the sink.

**The ceiling moved:** `UNC_COMMENT_MAX` was 255 (Compact Pro's byte length);
zip's is two bytes, so it is 65,535 and **a host may no longer size a fixed
buffer by it** — the CLI's `UNC_COMMENT_MAX * 3 + 1` stack array would be 192 KB
and now flushes in 384-byte pieces. A constant named for one format's field width
breaks a buffer far away when a second format shares the concept.

**Its own allocation, taken and released before the extraction buffers** (64 KB
is a real fraction of a 1 MB heap): the fixture's high-water stays 54,856 bytes.
A failed allocation or a length past EOF drops the comment and extracts the
archive.

**Graded by existing suites:** `run_diff.py` had excused a set holding `Zip`
from comparing `lsar`'s `XADComment`; deleting it was the change, and both halves
fail with delivery removed (verified). `tests/run_mac_sink.sh` grades the Mac's
`Comments` byte for byte on x86-64 and qemu-m68k. The unit test covers a comment
longer than Compact Pro allows, a length past EOF, and a host without the
callback.

## 2026-08-27 (a member over 2 GB) — the entry is not the archive

`fmt_exo.c` refused a tar member over 2 GB by ending the walk, which cost
every member behind it: a tar of `[4 KiB, 2.5 GiB, 11 B]` listed one file of
three. It is now a per-entry refusal — reported through the sink with a new
code, `UNC_ERR_TOOLARGE` — and the walk resumes where that member's own header
says the next one begins.

**A cap that ends a walk is only justified when the walk cannot continue.**
What genuinely ends a tar is the NEXT position leaving 32 bits (the 4 GB
container limit every format shares); that check moved to the advance,
*after* the member is reported, so the last member a header describes is still
named. `[1.5, 1.5, 1.5 GiB, small]` lists three of four and exits 1, the older
documented behaviour preserved. The advance is computed in 64 bits — a libgcc
call on a 68000, once per 512-byte header, nowhere near a decode loop.

**A new error code rather than `UNC_ERR_UNSUPPORTED`**, because that one prints
"this compression method is not supported yet" over a stored file and the CLI
then asks for the specimen — a 2.5 GB file, for a limit no specimen can
advance. A fourteenth negative is cheaper than a message that misdirects.

**Only tar can pose the question** — corrected 2026-08-27, same day: a zip
carrying Zip64 extra fields poses it too (*the Zip64 escape at 2 GB*). Every
other format in scope declares an entry's size in a 32-bit field; without a
Zip64 field zip's ceiling is the format's own, and the Macintosh formats
inherit HFS's 2 GB. The other `0x7FFFFFFF` guards in `src/` are not the same
rule — probe rejections decide recognition, and the segmented-set descriptors
in `fmt_sitseg.c` and `fmt_ddseg.c` describe one file, so refusing the set IS
the per-entry answer. Checked by editing a StuffIt fixture's second entry to
declare 0xFFFFFFFF and repairing the header CRC: it lists as `?`, fails alone,
the other eight are untouched. Without the CRC repair the reader refused at
the header, which measures the header check, not the size (FORMATS.md, *Size
limits*).

`tools/run_sizelimits.py` holds it in `ci.sh` on sparse subjects graded by GNU
tar (a 4.5 GB archive costs a few kilobytes because every oversized member is a
hole). That bounds what it proves: the holes are never read, so the read path
over a multi-gigabyte entry is unexercised, and unreachable on the Mac target.

## 2026-08-27 (the Zip64 escape at 2 GB) — a ceiling that was half what it said

A 3.4 GB zip of 23,400 entries **listed all 23,400 and then failed 21,352 of
them**, one per entry at or past 0x80000000. The documented ceiling was 4 GiB
and every offset fit in 32 bits.

**The boundary belongs to the WRITER, not to the format.** A central-directory
record whose local-header offset passes CPython's `ZIP64_LIMIT` — 2³¹ − 1, not
2³² − 1 — is written as `0xFFFFFFFF` with the real offset in extra field
0x0001. `fmt_exo.c` read only 0x9901 (WinZip AES), so it seeked to 0xFFFFFFFF
and returned `UNC_ERR_CORRUPT`. Info-ZIP 3.0 does not escape at all at 2.2 GB
(plain 32-bit offsets past 0x80000000), and 7-Zip orders the large member last.
"We read a zip up to 4 GiB" was true or false depending on the writing tool.

**Reading the escape costs no 64-bit arithmetic.** Any archive this engine can
open is under 4 GiB, so the high half is zero in every case that can arise; it
is read as two `uint32` halves as the end-of-central-directory record has been
since 2026-08-25, and a set high half refuses the entry. The fix is one
extra-field walk shared with the AES one — APPNOTE 4.5.3 fields appear only
where the matching directory field holds its escape, in a fixed order, so the
record is walked, not indexed (XADMaster's `XADZipParser.m` does the same, and
records that stopping at the first recognised field is a known bug).

**Per entry, one code for a size and a position.** The directory is intact, so
the refusal belongs to the entry. `UNC_ERR_TOOLARGE`'s message became *"entry is
past this engine's 32-bit reach"*: the old wording named the tar case only.

- **A limit measured on subjects you generated measures your generator.**
  `run_sizelimits.py` proves a 3 GiB zip entry at offset 0, where no writer
  emits an escape; `run_ziplarge.py` builds 70,000 entries in a few megabytes.
  Neither produced a large OFFSET, and both looked like coverage of "large zips".
- **The scope smell fired twice on one decision.** "Zip64 is out of scope" named
  64-bit addressing and was read as covering everything Zip64; on 2026-08-25 it
  hid an archive with too many entries, and it hid this for two days more. Ask
  which USES a scope decision refuses, once per use.

## 2026-08-27 (the name cap) — a clamp the host cannot see is a rename nobody asked for

A sweep for limits applied by CLAMPING rather than refusing found the biggest
in `UncEntryInfo`: `name` is `UNC_NAME_MAX` (255) bytes, and a 457-byte zip path
extracted as 255 bytes and **exited 0** while `unzip` showed all 457.

**Why not just carry the name.** `UncEntryInfo` is 346 bytes on the
68000 target (302 until the Finder metadata joined it, 2026-10-17;
measured, and re-measured every time the struct grew — the
"280 bytes" that stood in `fmt_lzh.c` was never right, and the "296"
this entry stated until 2026-09-03 stopped being right a few hours after
it was written, 2026-09-03, *the struct that grew after it was
measured*; FORMATS.md, *Name limits*, carries the figure)
and it travels on a 4 KB call stack; zip's own maximum would need 65,535 bytes.
The cap is right; being silent about it was not.

**The ENGINE does not refuse**, because the Mac application shortens every
component to 31 characters for HFS anyway, and an eight-deep tree of full-length
names sums past 255 bytes routinely; refusing would deny files the shell would
have named correctly. The engine reports — `UncEntryInfo.name_truncated`, and
`name_full_len` where the format states the length — and the host decides.

**The CLI does not refuse either** (maintainer's call, same day, overturning a
first version that failed the entry): **the Linux CLI is constrained by the
filesystem it writes to, exactly like the Mac client.** It extracts under the
shortened name, cuts components on UTF-8 boundaries at `pathconf(_PC_NAME_MAX)`,
numbers a collision the shortening caused (as an 8.3 volume's `~1`, `~2`), lists
every shortened name in an end-of-run notice, and exits 0. The one refusal left
is a path past `_PC_PATH_MAX`.

**The notice lists the original names** (corrected the same day on the
maintainer's point). The bytes are gone from `UncEntryInfo` but not from the
FORMAT when the cut is made — zip's directory is in memory, tar's `path[256]`
holds all 256, AppleSingle's name entry is on disk. So `UncOptions.long_name` is
a HOST buffer the engine fills where it can, and `name_truncated` reads 2 rather
than 1 to say so. The CLI passes 64 KB; the Mac shell passes NULL and pays
nothing.

**uuencode looked like the exception and was not.** Its `begin` line went
through our 96-byte line buffer — ours, not the format's — and the bytes are
streaming past when dropped; they are now kept in the host's buffer. **Ask
whether a limit is the format's or your own first**: three formats' "we cannot
know" was one line buffer. What cannot be recovered is a name dropped before
the engine held it (a zip directory over the allocator budget read one record at
a time; MIME's 512-byte header; btoa's 256-byte line): the notice gives the
length where stated and says *the rest was cut before it reached us*, and never
presents the shortened name as the archive's. Those three buffers set the same
flag. Deliberately silent: a segmented set's DESCRIPTOR name (it comes from the
host's filename) and the archive comment (dropped by an older decision).

**Saying so is not refusing.** A first over-4-GB diagnosis refused the file at
open and cost a capability — a tar's members under 4 GB list and extract — and
`run_sizelimits.py` failed within the hour. The walk goes on, with `0xFFFFFFFF`
(the largest size `UncIO` can state) handed over in place of a wrapped one.

**The host had three caps of its own.** The CLI's 512-byte name buffer cut
paths of accented components (255 bytes of MacRoman become up to 765 of UTF-8)
— now sized from `UNC_NAME_MAX`: a cap that cannot be met beats one that is
announced. `outdir/name` sat in 1024 bytes, now `PATH_MAX`. AppleSingle's
real-name entry was read into 64 bytes, missed by the first sweep because it is
spelled `sizeof tmp`: **the constant you grep for may not be the one written.**

**The general shape, third instance:** a CLAMP produces an internally
consistent result nothing downstream can notice — the zip entry count saturating
at 65,535 (2026-08-25), the Zip64 escape read as an offset (2026-08-27), and
this. When a constant meets archive data, ask "what happens to the archive that
exceeds it, and who is told".

## 2026-08-27 (the scaffolding audit) — the codec is the format, the code around it is not

Asked why there is so much per-format code: the **codecs** are as
format-specific as they look and should stay so; the **scaffolding** — staging,
checksumming and sinking decoded bytes, maintaining a folder path, deciding
whether an error is fatal to the walk — was written once per format. The
inventory and its closure are the two entries that follow.

**It is habit, not necessity**: each format was graded against an oracle, and
the cheapest correct move was a writer next to its codec; the fixtures pass
either way. The ORDER proves it — `unc_entry_path_append` and
`unc_entry_set_path` already existed when `DdPath`, `NowPath` and `SdPath` were
written beside them.

**A shared helper only helps the formats that call it.** The name-cut reporting
(*the name cap*) landed in `unc_entry_set_name` and `unc_entry_path_append`;
the three formats with their own path stack got only `name_truncated = 1` while
holding the components that would answer. **When a feature lands in a shared
helper, the list of who does NOT call it is the blast radius.** Same shape:
`env_is_envelope` and `IsEnvelopeFormat` were one predicate in two shells, and
disagreed for a day (2026-08-14).

**Four things that look like duplication and are not:**

- **Now Compress's whole-buffer decoders** (`now_lzss`, `now_newlzss`,
  `now_huffman`): the format is a table of blocks of at most 32 KB output
  against a 32 KB history, which is why its peak is a flat 128 KB; streaming
  would trade a measured constant for a worse one.
- **`SdLz`**: LSB-first WITHIN a 16-bit big-endian word, so
  `unc_bitin_init_le` would decode garbage. Its neighbour `SdHuff` IS the
  shared reader.
- **`ss_a3_sort`**: SpaceSaver's symbol order comes from the module's own
  non-stable quicksort and must be transcribed; the builder around it need not.
- **The codecs**: Arsenic, DDn, sit13, SlowFastA/B, the SpaceSaver methods.

**Why it is worth doing**: 932 fixtures byte-exact plus 9,320 robustness
variants make a scaffolding change pass-or-fail. Watch FORMATS.md's peak-RAM
matrix — a shared writer changes allocation shape, and a figure that does NOT
move after the change is a smell, not a reassurance.

**Landed the same day:** `unc_copy_fork` (three copies of a stored-fork loop),
`unc_fatal` (nineteen triage sites), `UncPath` (three path stacks and leaf
builders), `UncStage`, and `unc_format_is_envelope`. 460 lines out, 380 in, 932
fixtures byte-exact. No allocation touched, so peak RAM was not re-measured; the
stack was: largest frame unchanged, `dd_fork`/`dd_ddn` untouched, and the two
walks that had `*_path_leaf` inlined lost ~250 bytes of frame and gained one
288-byte call — a chain ~40 bytes deeper, against a 4 KB rule and a 3,290-byte
worst case elsewhere.

**The near-miss.** `ss_emit` and `sd_emit` matched for eight lines under an
identifier-normalising duplicate scan; SpaceSaver's also advances its sliding
window three lines past the match. Folding them compiled, sniffed and extracted
plausibly, and failed three unit tests on the preset dictionary. **A duplicate
detector reports a PREFIX, not a function** — read both to the closing brace.

**Two behaviour changes made `unc_fatal` worth more than its lines.** gzip
propagated no per-entry status and `.Z` omitted `UNC_ERR_IO`, so
`unc_gzip_extract` returned `UNC_OK` for a cancelled or I/O-failed decode —
both since M8, the two of nineteen sites where the predicate was written rather
than copied, and invisible through either host (both learn failure through
`end_entry`; the Mac shell tracks its own cancel). **A predicate spelled out at
nineteen sites has nineteen chances to be wrong, and no way for the odd one out
to look odd.**

## 2026-08-27 (the fork writer and the filter) — a shared hot path, measured three ways

The two large items from *the scaffolding audit*: `UncForkOut`, now the only
thing that stages decoded bytes and hands them to the sink, and `UncRle90`, the
only 0x90 run filter. 932 fixtures byte-exact, 9,320 robustness variants clean.
The first version of each was slower and the fixtures could not see it.

**The inventory was one short at each end**: ARC had a ninth fork writer inline
in `arc_entry_data` (found by reading `arc_emit`'s callers), and the audit had
called `ss_emit`/`sd_emit` one function. **Count by reading, not by scanning.**

**The cap is deliberately not in `UncForkOut`.** In each of the four formats
that stop at the declared length, the counter is ALSO the decode loop's own
condition (`o->left`, `r->remaining`, `s->want`, `t->outsize`), so hoisting it
would cost every other format a compare per byte for nothing.

**The filter went through three shapes and the fixtures liked all three.** A
callback cost a `.hqx` run **27 %** (gcc would not devirtualise it); an inlined
filter with a callback, 15 %. Removing the callbacks — inline `unc_rle90_feed`
and `unc_rle90_take`, each caller reading its own source — worked. Straight-lining
(10 %) and a fast/slow split like `UncBufIn` (4 %) were WORSE, because they grew
`bh_next` past gcc's inlining into `bh_fork`. The survivor costs 2-3 %.

**One instruction order was 2 % of a Compact Pro run.** `cpt_rle_emit`
decremented `r->remaining` before calling the writer where the original stored
first: +2.14 %, and swapping the two lines gave +0.04 %. **On a per-byte path,
measure the order too.**

**The net is a cost.** +0.86 % across a 14-fixture set (FORMATS.md, *Decode
cost*): BinHex +2.3 to +3.6 %, LZH +1.4 %, ARC +0.7 %, StuffIt and Compact Pro
unchanged, DiskDoubler **5.4 % faster** (`dd_out_byte` came out better). Stack:
`dd_fork` +44 B, deepest chain 3,334 B against a 4 KB rule. This simplification
was bought, not free.

**Two audit items are correctly unshared, settled by a number:**

- **SpaceSaver's Huffman builder must not become `UncCanon`.**
  `sizeof(UncCanon)` is **2,064 bytes** (mostly a 1 KB fast table that pays for
  itself on 256+ symbols); `SsA3` holds SEVEN tables, five of at most 32
  symbols rebuilt every block, so ~14 KB more on a method whose peak is a
  measured 41 KB, on a format that must fit the 1 MB floor.
- **`sd_huff_bit` must not become `UncBitIn`.** It refills 32 bits at a time and
  `sd_huff_end` derives where the next region begins from that cursor
  (`h->pos + 2`); a byte-granular reader would move it. This is the boundary
  OPEN_ITEMS.md records as open, where Alysis's 1991 and 1992 implementations
  disagree by one refill. (superseded: DECISIONS.md 2026-08-28, *the refill
  boundary* — the two implementations agree; the fault was this reader.)

## 2026-08-27 (the shapes that were left) — one probe signature, one scheme table, one buffer size

The last of the scaffolding audit: four places where the engine expressed a
per-format fact as a search instead of a table.

**Twenty-eight probes, three signatures, one reason.** `unc_sniff` was a
120-line `if` chain because probes differed: most took `(head, len)`, nine also
`io`, AppleSingle a `UncFormat *` to say which of two, and `unc_foreign_probe`
answered for ten formats — a probe that can answer for several cannot return a
flag. The signature is now

    UncFormat probe(const uint8_t *head, int32_t len, UncIO *io);

for all twenty-eight (unneeded `io` is ignored — the price of the array), and
`unc_sniff` walks `unc_sniff_order[]`, with the ordering arguments as comments on
their rows. `unc_formats[]` gained an extractor column, so `unc_extract_as`'s
26-case switch is a lookup, and three table scans share `unc_desc()`.

**`unc_appledouble_extract` lost an argument nobody read** (`(void)which;`);
both rows point at one function.

**The segment joiner's six `desc->scheme ==` tests were unnamed properties.**
One row per scheme now: `addressed`, `data_first`, `anonymous`, and slots for
`describe`, `match`, `payload`, `stored_crc` and `extract` — three filled by
DiskDoubler alone, which is what the `if (scheme == UNC_FORMAT_DDSEG)` tests hid.
`unc_segment_match` moved to `unc_segment.c`; its StuffIt half is
`unc_sitseg_match`.

**The audit was wrong about the hosts.** They dispatch on `scheme` to a
DIFFERENT question: which sibling FILE to look for (`.zip`, `.z01`, `.001`, a
`SPLT` part). That is filesystem naming, which the engine never touches — the
rule `UncVolumeSource` exists to keep. **Two dispatches on one enum are not
necessarily one dispatch.** It stays.

**`dd_fork` had its prologue nine times**, differing only in working memory;
that is now `dd_extra()`, and nine `unc_bufin_init` calls became three. Method 8
came OUT of the dispatch as `dd_fork_cpt`: it decodes through Compact Pro's
stage with its own writer and checksum.

**`4096` is `UNC_IOBUF`** — a bare literal in eleven files, named in one. A size
nobody chose is a size nobody can change.

**Free, measured:** +0.01 % instructions on the 14-fixture set; `dd_fork`'s
frame down 4 bytes, deepest chain 3,330 B (FORMATS.md, *Stack*). The audit's
list, OPEN_ITEMS.md's section 4, is gone.

## 2026-08-27 (the fast table StuffIt could not reach) — a gate that read as a property of the format

`unc_canon_decode`'s 10-bit lookup table (since M29) was gated on `!bi->le`,
with a comment that read like a fact about StuffIt method 13; it was a fact about
how the table is indexed.

**Cost, measured:** 58 instructions a symbol for Compact Pro, **189** for
StuffIt method 13. On `derived-Ultimate_Copland_1.1.sit.1`, `unc_canon_decode`
was 27,809,569 Ir over 146,952 symbols — 59 % of the run — and callgrind showed
the fast path executing **zero** times.

**So the window is turned round, not the table**: the peeked ten bits go through
a 256-byte const reversal table, and everything after is the existing code.
zlib's symbol-per-entry table needs no reversal but costs 2 KB more per
`UncCanon`, and DiskDoubler holds three at once and Now Compress two, inside
budgets FORMATS.md states to the byte.

**The first version was slower for everybody else.** A ternary peek and an `if`
consume put two branches per SYMBOL on the MSB path: Now Compress −2.56 %,
Compact Pro −1.87 %, LZH −2.65 %, −0.24 % overall — one format's 38 % paid for by
the rest. Hoisting the direction to one test at the top (two fast-path blocks)
gave −2.26 % overall with **every** `UncCanon` user faster. **A shared hot path
has no cheap `if`: ask how often each branch runs.**

**Two of three expected beneficiaries do not use this decoder.** SpaceSaver has
no `UncCanon` (its `SsHuff` is transcribed, *the fork writer and the filter*),
and ARC's Squeezed, Crushed and Distilled walk their own node arrays; `fmt_sit.c`
is the only LSB-first caller. Two of three fixtures moved 0.00 %. **"Reads
LSB-first" and "uses the shared decoder" are two lists, and I had intersected
them by eye.**

**Measured and not done here:** `arc_raw_byte` is 81 % of
`derived-INTRECHO.pak` (146 M Ir) at 129 instructions per output byte, walking
Distilled's tree a bit at a time (~10.5 steps a symbol; the bounds check alone
8.4 % of the run). How often each tree is rebuilt had to be measured first
(done in the next entry).

## 2026-08-27 (the tree that was walked a bit at a time) — ARC's Squeeze and Distilled get a first-bits table

ARC's Squeeze and Distilled store an explicit tree of node pairs and walked it
one bit at a time; `arc_raw_byte` was **81 % of the largest single run in the
corpus** (`derived-INTRECHO.pak`, 146 M Ir) at 129 instructions per output byte.

**The measurement the previous entry asked for**: on that fixture, **10 trees
for 295,185 symbols** (read once per ENTRY, not per block), and code lengths

| bits | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 | 11+ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| share | 13.2 % | 6.7 % | 4.9 % | 9.9 % | 18.3 % | 16.6 % | 19.9 % | 8.6 % | 1.8 % |

7.0 bits a symbol on average and **98.2 % ten or fewer**, so a ten-bit table
resolves nearly all in one lookup, with the walk as fallback.

**Indexed raw — the opposite of the StuffIt case an hour earlier.** Both
streams are LSB-first, but `unc_canon_decode` assembles codes MSB-first and must
reverse its window, while ARC's walk takes the first bit as the first branch.
**The bit order of the STREAM and the order a code is ASSEMBLED in are different
questions.**

**The builder runs the decoder's own walk**: each tree has a `step` function
(child, leaf, bad) shared by walk and builder, and the table is filled by
walking all 1,024 window values, so the table cannot disagree with the walk.

**One divergence nearly got in**: the first Squeeze fast path checked only the
256 end code where the walk also refuses anything above 255 — caught by reading,
the second fast path in two days to drop a refusal (`ss_emit` reached CI).
**When a fast path replaces a walk, list what the walk REFUSES.**

**Result, over the 48-fixture set:**

| | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `derived-INTRECHO.pak` | 146,326,346 | 89,159,573 | **−39.07 %** |
| `synth-arc-mixed.arc` | 2,040,944 | 1,960,599 | −3.94 % |
| ARC's LZW methods | | | 0.00 %, no tree to walk |
| **TOTAL** | 1,078,346,090 | 1,021,099,385 | **−5.31 %** |

**Cost.** +654 B of `fmt_arc.o` text; +2,560 B heap for a Distilled entry, +2,048
B for Squeeze; +8 B stack. ARC's documented 46.5 KB peak is **unmoved**:
bisected over every `.arc` and `.pak` fixture, 46,686 B before and after, set by
`arc2pak1.pak`, an LZW method.

**With the three tiers and both decoders:** 1,098,529,621 Ir before the
harmonisation, **1,021,099,385** after — **−7.05 %** over the two largest
fixtures of every format.

## 2026-08-27 (what the tables left behind) — the profile moves, and the next thing is never the thing on the list

`unc_bitin_bit`'s per-bit `if (b->le)` (~1.1 % of a Compact Pro run, third on a
list) is **no longer worth doing**: the two tables removed the bit-at-a-time
traffic and it is absent from the top of every profile. **A ranked list is only
ranked against the profile it was made on; re-profile after each one.**

**What re-profiling found.** The largest run is now Now Compress at 424 M Ir,
4.5 % of it the CONDITION of two decode loops: `now_bit_offset()` ran once per
symbol (1,993,952 times on `derived-SyntheticReferences2.0.sea`) calling
`unc_bufin_tell()` and multiplying. A `NowBits` is always memory-backed, so
`lenfed == len` and the call recovered `pos`. One line: **−2.33 %** on that
fixture, −0.73 % on `synth-now-mixed.now`.

**Measured and NOT taken, both for spending the scarce resource:**

- **A symbol per `UncCanon` fast-table entry** (zlib's shape): ~64 → ~55
  instructions a symbol, ~4 % of a Now Compress run, for 2 KB per table, with
  Now Compress holding two and DiskDoubler three against peaks stated to the
  byte for a 1 MB machine. The maintainer's to reverse, not a profile's.
- **Slice-by-4 CRCs**: `unc_crc32` is 6.8 % of a Compact Pro run,
  `unc_crc16_arc` 9.2 % of a StuffIt one; 2-3× faster for tables of 1 KB → 4 KB
  — code, not heap, but 3 KB on a 177 KB application for a few percent of two
  formats.

**The whole sequence:** over the two largest fixtures of every format,
**1,098,529,621 Ir before the harmonisation, 1,011,192,657 after it and the
three decoder changes — −7.95 %**, with the engine 2 KB smaller on the target.
