## 2026-08-27 (the path builder's own cap) — the bytes were still in the walk

`unc_path_leaf` reported a cut name without the name, and with the wrong length:
a nine-deep Now Compress tree of 31-byte components is a 296-byte path, and the
notice said *287 bytes; the rest was cut before it reached us* — both false. The
helper had cut into its own 255-byte buffer on the way DOWN.

**The fix is where the bytes still are.** DiskDoubler, Now Compress and
SuperDisk! hold every component in a header the walk is still reading. `UncPath`
now carries the uncut LENGTH and writes the uncut BYTES straight into
`UncOptions.long_name` as it descends (`full` is both length and write offset, so
a pop restores both); a host with no buffer (the Mac shell) pays one addition per
component, and no second engine buffer exists.

**A second defect one layer down.** `unc_extract_as`, given no `UncOptions`,
zeroed *a list of fields* written when the struct had nine members, so
`long_name` — added that day — was read off an uninitialised stack for every
in-tree caller; harmless until three formats asked for it, then the unit tests
segfaulted at `-O2` and passed under ASan at `-O1`. It zeroes the whole struct
now. **A per-field initialiser is a list nothing tells you has stopped being
complete.**

**Why nothing found it for months**: the three formats' fixtures have short
paths, and the suite that reaches the cap generates zip, tar, uuencode and
AppleSingle — ONE long name — and said so in its docstring (*"nothing here
synthesises such a container"*). **A named blind spot in a passing suite is a
bug report with no reproduction attached.** `tools/synth_now.py` writes the
container; `unar`, which has no cap, gives the intended path.

## 2026-08-28 (the OS 9 tier's last three keystrokes) — a run that stopped early still reported every step it took

The Mac OS 9 harness had never driven the application past the destination
dialog. After launch it sent Return, Return, Cmd-Q; the second Return accepts
the **destination** dialog, so `14-result.png` was SFPutFile, "extraction
reported" had timed that dialog opening, and Cmd-Q went into Standard File,
where it means nothing. The verdict (read off the volume, 20/20) stood; every
claim about where the run had got to was wrong. **A harness that stops early
still reports every step it took**, each with a plausible number. Fix: name a
shot after what is in it, and add the missing steps (dismiss the alert, check
SFGetFile repaints, Cmd-. to leave).

**The completion wait changed with it.** `wait_change` fires on the progress
dialog's ten-a-second repaint; waiting for STILLNESS reported a 30 s extraction
done at 14 s, because "0%  estimating time left" is still until the first
percent. **Stillness is a proxy for "done"** (as `settle()` learned 2026-08-02).
The replacement is a state signature: the dialog's TITLE LINE, which changes
only when the dialog is replaced.

**One keystroke is not a test of a keystroke.** One Cmd-. failed to cancel; on a
DIFFERENT archive the first chord cancelled (1 of 34 entries, byte-exact, 33
never started); three more on the original did nothing. The variable was the
archive's format.

**The cause was in the engine since the format was written.** `ProgressPump()`
runs only from the progress callback, and `src/fmt_now.c` read blocks with
`unc_read_full` on the raw `UncIO`, so **Now Compress never called the callback
at all** — the dialog sat at 0% and Cancel was unreachable for the whole entry.
One `unc_progress_add` per block fixes it (interval at most `NOW_INBLOCK` = 32
KB, now in include/macextract.h); same archive, same harness: the first Cmd-.
cancels, 1 of 2 entries written, byte-exact.

**Nothing could have seen it**: every `ci.sh` suite grades bytes, and 946
fixtures passed without the header's contract being checked once.
`tools/tick_probe.c` and `tools/run_ticks.py` now measure it per fixture: fails
on the pre-fix engine, passes on this one, and reports the widest gap (30,634 B
with Now Compress's block tick; 16,172 B without it). **A property nothing
measures is not protected, however often it is written down.** The harness now
repeats Cmd-. until the dialog goes, prints the count, and prints "Cmd-. DID NOT
CANCEL" — **a negative indistinguishable from a lost keystroke is not a test.**

**The cancel pass condition** has no oracle, so it asserts a shape: a **strict,
non-empty subset** of entries, each byte-exact, nothing left by the in-flight
entry. Both degenerate outcomes fail as a broken TEST and name a better archive.

**And the cheap observation that was there all along**: the run had never
reached the Finder after quit, where PackIt's `App` + MacRoman `CC A9` (already
in the OS 9 sample) is drawn as `AppÃ©` in icon view and in Standard File — the
same two characters the Linux CLI prints as UTF-8. Every tier compares the
bytes; only the two Mini vMac ones had photographed the glyphs.

## 2026-08-28 (clicking a dialog that does not exist yet) — park the pointer before the thing you mean to hit appears

The progress dialog's Cancel BUTTON (the `DialogSelect` branch of
`ProgressPump()`, beside Cmd-.) had never been clicked on Mac OS 9: `goto()`
costs ~40 s and the dialog lives seconds.

**Position early against a stationary predecessor.** The button's position is
known from `mac/macextract.r` (`DLOG` 128 does not autocentre; item 1 of `DITL`
128 is at (340,168)), and the destination dialog before it waits forever — so the
pointer is parked there during SFPutFile, and the click is instantaneous.

Two details, each of which would have read as "the button does nothing":

- **The press is HELD, 0.9 s.** `TrackControl` asks whether the button is still
  down; an application pumping events from its progress callback dequeues the
  mouseDown a tick late, and a 60 ms tap reads as released outside.
- **The guest gets a relative `usb-mouse`**; the fixture run's tablet is inert
  (BLOCKERS.md, *Withdrawn claims*).

**The control is the whole result.** `--click-at 150,168` presses the same
dialog's blank background, 190 px away: the button cancels on the first press (1
of 34, byte-exact), the background does not (34 of 34, failing as a late
cancel). That separates "the button works" from "a click works". Numbers in
FORMATS.md, *Cancelling, and an 8-bit name*; re-running in `tools/vmac/README.md`.
The positioning code moved to `os9mouse.Pointer` rather than being copied.

## 2026-08-28 (the password dialog on Mac OS 9) — a change threshold is only as good as the rectangle it is measured over

Decryption on Mac OS 9 was filed as a harness limitation, but the dialog is
keyboard work (`PassFilter`: Return = OK, Escape = Cancel). What was missing was a
subject: **nothing in the corpus is encrypted**, measured (FORMATS.md,
*Encryption*), so `--encrypted` generates one as `interactive.py --password`
does — StuffIt classic DES, whose verifier `'MKey'` 0 is in the RESOURCE fork
(MacBinary on Linux, the File Manager on the Mac). Three entries byte-exact,
resource forks included. **The wrong password goes first** (an application that
ignored the password would otherwise pass); photographed: `wrongone`, then "That
password was refused."

**The transferable part.** The refusal step reported *"NO CHANGE, continuing
anyway"* — 0.43 % over a 120 s timeout — while the screenshot showed it. The
rectangle was `WINDOW_RECT`, 600x500; over the message area from `DITL` 132 the
same event is **19 % in 4 s**. When a threshold disagrees with a photograph,
suspect the rectangle: **an aggregate cannot fail on a property it averages
away.**

## 2026-08-28 (the exception one front end had) — a rule implemented in one shell is not implemented

Replaying SpaceSaver on Mac OS 9 (its specimens are Aladdin's own, made under
`qemu-m68k`, uncommittable, run by path): 76,800 B byte-exact (FORMATS.md).

**It found a Macintosh shell defect.** Nameless formats take the archive's
filename "minus its last extension" (as `unar` does), except SpaceSaver, which
compresses IN PLACE and adds no extension. `cli/main.c` said so in a comment;
`mac/macextract_mac.c` stripped unconditionally, so `Report.txt` came out as
`Report` on the Mac only. No suite saw it: the Mini vMac tiers compare CRC sums
and counts, and the one tier that compares names had never had this format.
**Where two front ends must agree, the agreement needs a test that fails.**

**The reconciliation strengthened the tier**: an in-place format's output is
named after the archive, so the Mac writes `archive.sit~1` beside it while Linux
writes `archive.sit`; `verify_output()` maps one to the other, and the
NOT_OUTPUT guard no longer refuses the fixture. An overwritten archive still
reads as no output; extension-stripping reads as one missing and one unexpected
file.


## 2026-08-28 (the walk nobody had descended) — writing the container is what tests the walk

`src/fmt_dd.c`'s two directory walks (`DDAR` isdir/enddir records, `DDA2`'s
dirlevel counter), transcribed from XADMaster, had never descended a tree;
OPEN_ITEMS.md named the remedy, a writer `unar` could grade.

`tools/synth_dd.py` is that writer. The records are twenty lines of
`struct.pack`; the work was the CRC-16/XModem over the first 76 bytes (`DDAR`),
60 (`DDA2`) or 82 (a 0xABCD0054 file header) that `recognizeFileWithHandle`
checks — without it `unar` cannot recognise the archive and the generator grades
nothing, while this magic-only engine reads everything. **A generator must
satisfy the oracle's recogniser, a part of the format the extractor may ignore.**
The algorithm came from the specimens (XADMaster's table is 0x1021 byte-swapped,
compared byte-swapped: plain XModem stored big-endian), verified on all nine.

**The same bullet named SuperDisk!'s up-directory record as untested** — but
`super-disk-utility.hqx` walks two folders and pops between them, adjudicated
against its own self-extractor (`tools/run_superdisk.py`). Only DEPTH is untested
(BLOCKERS.md). **An "untested" claim is about the corpus and expires with it.**


## 2026-08-28 (the front end that was already doing it) — read the shell, not the flag

OPEN_ITEMS.md asked for "`~1` numbering in `mac/macextract_mac.c`"; it has been
there since M10, keyed off the File Manager's `dupFNErr`, which catches every
collision the 31-character cut creates without the engine's flag (BLOCKERS.md).

**What the shell lacks is the notice — a screen decision, so it stayed open.**
Measured: two FOLDERS that shorten alike MERGE (`EnsureDir` descends into the
existing one, as the Finder would), and a path the engine had to cut lands in its
parent folder, numbered. Nothing is lost; nobody is told.

**Where the test went**: `tests/mac_sink_test.c` has run the real shell since
M10; what was missing was an archive reaching the caps, which
`tools/synth_dd.py` now writes. **A front end is not tested by reading it** —
three one-line breakages of the shell fail this suite three different ways.


## 2026-08-28 (the refill boundary) — the specimen that could not be made, made

OPEN_ITEMS.md wanted a real block whose coded flag bitstream is a multiple of 32
bits, and said sizing a subject cannot produce one "because the 1991 panel codes
the flags one bit each" — both from four subjects sized `ceil(size/8) % 4 == 0`.

**That rule describes the harness's own flat 8-bit encoder.** The panel writes a
real Huffman code per flag BYTE. Measured (`tools/sdhuff.py`, the
`fmt_superdisk.c` reader with a counter): 130, 133, 260 and 261 bits for 125,
128, 255 and 256 flag bytes — **nflags + 5** — so the aim is
`ceil(ulen/8) + 5 ≡ 0 (mod 32)`: 1240 bytes lands on 160 bits, 2008 on 256; 1248
and 2016 are one bit past, as controls.

**The panel wrote all four, and this engine got the two on the boundary wrong
from byte 0.** The reading was ours; the two Alysis implementations agree and
always did (BLOCKERS.md). **The fix is in the READER, not the `+ 2`**:
`sd_huff_bit` fetches a long only when a bit is asked for, the compressor's
reader already has it, so `sd_huff_end`'s cursor is four bytes further on when the
last symbol ends exactly on a refill. Writing the four into the constant would
have been right for these blocks and wrong for every other.

**Lessons**: `run_sdmodule.py` SKIPPED every synthetic block reaching the
boundary — a tolerance resting on our own output, skipping the one case that
would catch this. And a measurement missing its target (by 2 to 5 bits) was
written up as a property of the format rather than of the arithmetic.


## 2026-08-28 (the tree count) — a probe outside the legal range tests the range check

Method 5's leading byte was confirmed only at 0, and "a count of 16 is rejected
by both expanders" was read as *possibly our reading is wrong*. **It was
neither.** `CODE` 11 of the 1991 `DiskDoubler™ App` (on the 3.1.2 floppy already
kept) validates the count first:

    1dfc:  cmpiw #32   -> valid      1e10:  cmpiw #128  -> valid
    1e08:  cmpiw #64   -> valid      1e18:  cmpiw #256  -> valid
                                     else   moveq #0    -> invalid

The decompressor at 0x228c turns 0 into 256, answers -20999 on an invalid count
and -20998 when it exceeds the trees allocated (it allocates `count * 1536` and
HALVES the count down to 32 while allocation fails), and masks the next context
with `count - 1` at 0x1fbc — `byte % count` for all four legal values, which is
what `enc_splay` writes. A 128-tree fork came back **byte-exact from that
expander** (`ddencode.py --expand`), and the 16-tree one is asserted REFUSED.

**A value outside the legal range exercises the range check, and says nothing
about the reading it was aimed at.** The disassembly took twenty minutes on a
disk image kept since 2026-08-21, while the item waited for a specimen nobody
could produce — in the expander already used as the oracle.

## 2026-08-28 (`--only`) — an exemption keyed to a proxy is an exemption that misfires

`--only NAME` restricts `l`, `x` and `t` to the entries named.

**The selector is the name `l` prints**, compared after `name_to_fs`, so a
listing row is a selector (the Finder's icon file is `Icon\r`, CR included).
**A selector that matches nothing is an error**, not a silent exit 0; every match
is recorded, which makes the report possible.

**The envelope exemption is keyed to the unwrap GATE, not the format.** `x`
peels `.hqx`/`.bin`/`.gz` on the way to the archive, so a layer about to be
unwrapped is exempt. The first version asked `layer_unwraps(fmt)`, but `l` and
`t` never unwrap, so `--only` was silently inert there (a typo'd selector on
`macextract t archive.sit.bin` exited 0). The condition is now the auto-unwrap's
own expression via one shared helper. **Key an exemption to the condition it
protects, not to something usually true alongside it.**

A claim corrected before it was built on: "no host has ever returned >0 from
`begin_entry`" was wrong — listing returns it for every entry and BOTH hosts for
every directory (`sink_begin` in `cli/main.c` and `mac/macextract_mac.c`). What
had never happened is the MIXED case while writing, which found Now Compress and
DiskDoubler calling `end_entry` for a skipped folder against `macextract.h`'s
contract. That question was one grep of two files.

## 2026-08-28 (three ideas, two numbers) — a constant nobody named cannot be searched for

The engine had **42 raw `0xFFFFFFFF` / `0x7FFFFFFF` literals across 14
source files** and one named ceiling, `UNC_SIZE_UNKNOWN`; `grep 0xFFFFFFFF` mixed
CRC-32's initial value, a zip escape, a StuffIt 5 marker, register masks and the
addressing ceiling. Three ceilings, now named apart:

| name | value | the idea |
|---|---|---|
| `UNC_OFF_MAX` | 0xFFFFFFFF | what `UncIO` can address — `seek`/`tell`/`size` are `uint32` |
| `UNC_MAC_MAX` | 0x7FFFFFFF | what a classic Macintosh file can be — HFS caps a fork at 2 GB, and the File Manager's position parameter is a signed long |
| `UNC_READ_MAX` | 0x7FFFFFFF | the largest single read the engine expresses — `UncIO.read` takes an `int32_t` |

Plus three non-limits: `UNC_CRC32_INIT`, `ZIP64_ESC32`, `SIT5_DATALEN_NONE`.

What naming exposed:

- **`UNC_SIZE_UNKNOWN` and `UNC_OFF_MAX` are the same number** — the first thing a
  widened offset type would break silently.
- **`0x7FFFFFFF` meant two things in `fmt_exo.c`**: a tar member's fork ceiling
  and a central-directory read length.

Behaviour is unchanged by construction, which the 932-fixture suite can prove;
it could not prove a widening — a `unc_off_t` 64-bit on Linux and 32-bit on 68k
would be **two engines and one differential suite**, every `high half is set`
guard compiled out where tested and live where shipped. (superseded:
DECISIONS.md 2026-08-28, *what a width costs* — the 32-bit build grades on
Linux.)

**No codec file mentions `UncIO` at all** (`unc_inflate.c`, `unc_lzw.c`,
`unc_lzah.c`, `unc_lzdyn.c`, `unc_huffman.c`, `sit_arsenic.c`, `unc_crypt.c`); all
~64 `seek`/`tell`/`size` sites are in parsers, a handful per entry, so a wider
offset's 68000 cost is not in the decompressors.

Four literals stay raw on purpose — SuperDisk!'s three `& 0xFFFFFFFF` register
masks and Arsenic's range-coder overflow guard, fixed by the algorithm; if the
offset type widens, they must NOT follow.

## 2026-08-28 (what a width costs) — the offset type is a compile-time choice, not an architecture

`UncIO` carries a container offset in `unc_off_t`: `uint32_t` by default,
`uint64_t` under `UNC_OFF64`. **The abstraction costs the 68000 nothing; the wider
type costs it 0.5 %.**

`m68k-apple-macos-size`, same toolchain and flags:

| build | text | data |
|---|---|---|
| before, `uint32_t` spelled out | 138,868 | 31,440 |
| `unc_off_t` = 32-bit — what ships | 138,864 | 31,412 |
| `unc_off_t` = 64-bit, on 68k | 139,576 | 31,436 |

Both widths pass 683 unit checks, 932 fixtures and 9,320 robustness variants
under ASan+UBSan. A 6 GiB tar of four 1.5 GiB members: GNU tar lists four, the
32-bit build three (exit 1), the 64-bit build four (exit 0).

**The previous entry's objection was wrong**: width is a compile-time choice, so
the 32-bit configuration builds and grades on Linux against the same oracle —
`ci.sh` variant 5 — without which two widths would not be defensible.

- **`-Wconversion` finds only half a widening**: 24 sites narrowing a widened
  value, but never a 32-bit local passed INTO a widened `seek`; tar's walk was
  widened by hand.
- **Only tar gains**: its positions are a running sum. zip past 4 GiB is Zip64
  ADDRESSING, out of scope (OPEN_ITEMS.md part 1).
- **Widen only what addresses.** Entry sizes stay 32-bit; the classic formats keep
  32-bit addressing behind `unc_io_size32()`, which clamps a container past 4 GiB
  to "length not stated", the leniency a streamed container gets.
- **A test asserting a ceiling must ask the binary which it has.**
  `run_sizelimits.py` failed the 64-bit build; `--version` now derives the width
  from `sizeof(unc_off_t)` and the test grades against that.

On the hardware: **69/69 on an emulated Mac Plus at 4 MB and 69/69 at the 1 MB
floor target**, System 6.0.8, `tools/vmac/sample.txt`. And `UNC_OFF64` on an
emulated Mac Plus: **69/69 PASS**, **identical peak heap on every one of the 69**
and identical grids (exact integers). "It would never be run there" was a scope
statement wearing a technical one; `mac/CMakeLists.txt` carries the switch.

**Time is not measured, because of the instrument.** `macburger-helper.hqx` at
1x, alternating 32/64/32/64: **104.0, 104.0, 104.1, 104.1 s**, but `run.py`
timestamps at 3 s polls, so the result is **"no difference above 3 %", not a
stopwatch**; every reachable subject is decode-dominated, and a parser-bound one
(tens of thousands of entries) does not fit a 1440 KB floppy. On the host,
500,000 entries LISTED cost 0.17-0.18 s at either width — which says nothing
about m68k. The true 68k cost is under 3 %, with +0.51 % of text the only hard
number.

**Build hazard, not fixed here** (first diagnosis wrong: `ENGINE_HDR` does list
the headers, since 2026-08-23): **make tracks timestamps, not flags**, so adding
`UNC_OFF64` without `make clean` links a mixed build. `ci.sh` cleans between
variants; the Makefile says so where `OFFDEFS` is defined.

## 2026-08-28 (the certificate painted first) — a completion marker that goes down first certifies nothing

Two of thirteen fixtures FAILed at `--poll 3` on a 4 MB Mac Plus and passed at
`--poll 20`. The README's hypothesis (a poll landing mid-paint, "a different
regime" at 4 MB) was wrong on both halves.

`at_report` erases to white, paints three calibration squares, then the 16-bit
sync word, then eight 32-bit values MSB-first. **The sync word went down first**,
so a mid-paint frame decoded cleanly with unreached cells reading zero. The kept
frame proves it exactly: `derived-PackIt.pit` reported `totalRsrcLen`
**0x00008000** where the truth is **0x0000DB05** (painting stopped after bit 17)
and `peakBytes` 0; `ret` was already 0, so the host took it as final.

**The sync word is now painted last** — a completion certificate: a mid-paint
frame has no sync, `decode_grid.py` rejects it, and the host looks again. Both
fixtures pass at `--poll 3` and `--poll 1`.

- **A "this is complete" marker must be written after what it describes**;
  written first it is a header, which cannot tell complete from interrupted.
- **"Poll more slowly" hid a defect for weeks**, and the two rows it forced to
  `--poll 20` are the coarsest in FORMATS.md's timing table. A tolerance widened
  to silence a symptom is worth re-opening.
- **Look at the image**: the mechanism came from decoding the one frame the
  harness had kept all along.

## 2026-08-29 (the yardstick) — the free tool, run at last

The comparison with StuffIt Expander 4.0.2 had been Aladdin's documentation
against our measurements for two weeks; what was missing was a download and
about forty minutes of emulator. Results: FORMATS.md, *Timed on the same Mac
Plus*.

**The clock has to be outside both applications, and the quiet period is not
part of the answer.** Our own `startTicks` against screen polling for Expander
(~50 ms a poll) would have measured the harness, so both are timed by
screenshot, reporting the **last frame that differed from the one before it**,
not the total wait (proving the work stopped takes a minute of unchanged
screen). The residual error is one poll interval, paid by both, which is why
the ratio is quoted and the seconds are not.

**"The volume is empty" was a fact about our own sink.** Expander expanded a
278 KB archive for 56 seconds, photographed at "Items remaining to UnStuff:
3", and the image afterwards held nothing. Our sink calls `FlushVol` after
each fork; Expander leaves its writes in the File Manager's cache, and
SIGKILLing the emulator discards them. **An instrument inherits its
assumptions from the one subject it has always had.** Command-Q after the
measurement fixed it at no cost to the comparison.

**Mixed was the useful outcome.** Expander unstuffs StuffIt in three quarters
of our time; we expand Compact Pro in five sixths of its, and a BinHex
envelope with an archive inside in under two thirds. One fixture would have
supported whichever conclusion it landed on — the argument for one fixture
per format. The times are comparable only because both applications wrote the
same output names on every fixture.

## 2026-08-29 (SuperDisk! method 13) — the specimen that would have settled nothing

OPEN_ITEMS.md filed method 13 under *"waiting on a file this machine does not
have"*, closable by **"a file that actually contains one"**. That was wrong
twice over.

**The method table is real, and 13 is in it.** Disk Expander 1.2's INIT 32
compress path (@0x5232) indexes an eleven-entry table at +0xf2e, eight bytes
per entry: 1, 11, 17, 2, 18, 12, 1, 11, 11, 1 and **13**. Three of those (12,
17, 18) have no module in this product — method 20's lesson again: **the
number identifies a codec in a library, and the library is not this
product's.**

**But the file would have settled nothing: there is nothing to grade it
against.** Module 13 answers command 2 and executes `_Debugger` on decompress,
at its own 0xd4 (SIGILL under the runner). Alysis's extension hands method 9
and up to the module of that number, so no shipped expander can read a method
13 block. Four streams written here decode as no method this engine or the
other modules know. Specimens can now be made at will; a second reader cannot.

So the item moves to Part 1. Module 13 IS a reference implementation and
inverting it is legitimate under rule #1, but the result would be a decoder
for a codec no Alysis expander reads, that no corpus archive uses, with
nothing to check it against.

### Verified afterwards: the number is a slot, and eDisk proves it

The deleted OPEN_ITEMS.md entry also claimed eDisk 1.2 and More Disk Space 1.1
"carry only methods 1, 11 and a 13 named ' Copy'", citing DECISIONS.md
2026-08-25 and `tools/vmac/rescomp.py`. **Neither source mentions either
product.** Checked by downloading both (Macintosh Garden, md5s in FORMATS.md):

- **eDisk 1.2's module 13 is a byte copier.** `Cmpr` 0 and 1, resource name
  `JC`, module name " Copy", 310 B and 290 B, working buffer zero, an unrolled
  `MOVE.B (A0)+,(A1)+`.
- **More Disk Space 1.1 is where the claim was wrong.** Its `Alysis
  Preferences` carries 1, 2, 9, 10, 11 twice and a `Cmpr` 26 named SlowFastC
  declaring 5,030 B — Disk Expander's module 13, not eDisk's.

**A claim can be true and still have no evidence behind it where it says it
does.** In 1992 slot 13 held a byte copier; by 1993, in another product, a
codec wanting 229,618 bytes of buffer. A block header's "13" means nothing
without knowing which library wrote it — and this project read it as a method
for six days.

### The transferable part: a guard is not a requirement

FORMATS.md said module 13 "wanted a 64 KB working buffer (it compares
`workingBufferSize` against 65536 and DEBUGGERs below it)" — true, and only a
floor in the module's code. What it needs is the long at +0x1E of its header,
229,618 bytes, which INIT 32 checks before calling (@0x51a2, -4 below). Given
64 KB it died on every input, and the crash was then blamed on the module.
**A guard says "not below this"; a manifest says "this much".** The runner now
takes the larger of its heuristic and the module's declaration — no change for
methods 1-11, the whole difference for 13.

## 2026-08-29 (methods 3, 4 and 5, graded across the format) — the gap was in our encoder

OPEN_ITEMS.md wanted *"a DiskDoubler fork of method 3, 4 or 5 that this
project did not write"*, because nothing graded "the encodings our encoder
does not emit". **Those encodings were missing from our ENCODER, and the
expander does not care who wrote the stream.**

`ddencode.py` has handed forks to Salient's 1991 DiskDoubler since
2026-08-21, so the fix was to emit what our encoder never had. Five cases, one
boot (FORMATS.md, *What the 1991 expander accepts*): method 5 at 32 and 64
trees and a method 4 tree with a depth-1 leaf, byte-exact; `ESC 2`, the
shortest run, byte-exact; `ESC 1` refused twice. **A specimen grades one set
of shapes; this grades the range** — the second time this month the *"what
would close it"* line was what was wrong (SuperDisk! method 13, above).

### The control is the whole reason the first answer is not in the docs

The first run refused BOTH new method 3 cases — but both forks had GROWN (564
bytes in, 767 and 567 out), which an expander may refuse on sight: the Splay16
mistake (DECISIONS.md 2026-08-28). With a 3,000-byte run added and a
`RleGrow` control (grows, uses no new token): `Rle2` byte-exact, `RleGrow`
refused, `ESC 1` still refused. **When a probe and a control disagree about
which property is measured, the control is cheaper than the argument.**

### And the one that was a real divergence

`ESC 1` at offset 0 is two hypotheses; `RleEsc1Mid` puts it 1,800 bytes in
and is refused too, so it is the token. `dd_rle` passed `strict = 0` to the
shared RLE90 filter, after macutils — **the only one of six call sites that
did** (StuffIt, ARC twice, BinHex twice pass 1). A comment citing a reference
reads as sourced; nobody asked whether that reference was the vendor. The
engine now refuses; 91/91 DiskDoubler fixtures are unchanged.

## 2026-08-29 (four more names) — one of the five references was already here

**Superseded 2026-10-18** (*the formats it only named*): the four are not
recognised any more; their references grade `tools/run_foreign.py`'s
specimens.

OPEN_ITEMS.md carried *"Five archive formats are still unnamed for want of a
reference: zstd, lzip, brotli, lrzip and WIM"*. Four were named; the fifth
never can be.

**lzip's reference was in `reference/deark` the whole time** — `unsupported.c`
tests `LZIP` at offset 0, and deark had been here since 2026-08-25. **A "we
have no reference for X" list is a search, and a search is a claim about
somebody's looking** (BLOCKERS.md; the fourth time here).

**brotli cannot be identified, and that is a finding.** RFC 7932 section 9.1:
the stream header is one to seven bits of WBITS — no magic, no length. It
moves to part 1 with the RFC as evidence for a negative.

### What the weakest probe is allowed to be

lzip's magic is four ASCII bytes (deark rates it 50 against xz's 90). A sniff
returns one answer, so the confidence is spent on ORDER: lzip is tested after
every corroborated magic. The false positive is measured: a text file opening
with LZIPPER is claimed as lzip — worth it to somebody holding a `.lz`.

The other three are corroborated, each tested by removing it: zstd's
skippable-frame range (one value above and below), lrzip's `MAGIC_LEN`
(rejects a 23-byte file starting `LRZI`), WIM's header size (rejects 207,
wimlib accepts only 208).


## 2026-08-29 (the end-of-run report) — what the run cost, on a screen with no scrollback

The Mac application ended every run in one sentence ("Extraction complete." /
"Some entries could not be extracted."), naming neither renames nor failures;
the CLI had listed both since 2026-08-27. Decided: one box with both.

**A box only when there is something to say.** Otherwise the usual alert. The
outcome chain is one `if` ladder; box and alert are two ways of showing it.

**The outcome is the list's last line, and it is pinned.** As an ordinary
last line, a Mac Plus put "Extraction complete." nine rows below the fold on
an archive of eighteen photographs; as a static item below the frame the box
stopped reading as one document. What ships: after a blank line, same frame
and font, bold, held on the bottom row when the list overflows.

**The extension is KEPT and the stem is cut**, the collision number before it:
`LongDocumentName.txt` → `LongDocumen.txt`, `dup.txt` → `dup~1.txt`. **This
was decided backwards first** for a few hours (a Mac opens by type/creator, so
a suffix is decoration). Corrected because it is the FILE's convention that
matters: a name with a suffix generally came off a system with no Finder
types, so the archive holds none to stamp and the suffix is all that says what
opens it. The CLI's 255 bytes rarely needs the room.

**The verdict is worded for whether the list is there**: above a list naming
each failure, "Extraction finished."; the alert is unchanged.

**A name goes in whole, and the box wraps it.** Fixed-width lines elided at 36
characters said the same thing eighteen times for names differing at character
34. Text is packed in one pool and wrapped once when the box opens
(`TextWidth` is a trap call; scrolling must not pay it), breaking after the
name.

**Failures have 16 of the 64 lines reserved, and 1 KB of the pool.** The pool
is fixed (the engine budget is taken from `FreeMem()` once); filled in order,
100 alike names pushed out the entries that could not be written at all.

**A folder MERGED into another is reported, only where the archive declares
the folder.** The shell remembers the first 63 bytes of the archive's name for
up to 24 folders it made; folders that exist only inside paths are not guessed
at.

### Two defects, found by driving the box rather than by testing the lines

`interactive.py --report` builds an archive designed to make the report say
everything (long names, a duplicate, folders that shorten alike, eighteen
names alike for 31 characters, one damaged entry), extracts it on an emulated
Mac Plus, photographs and scrolls the box, saves it and reads the document
back. Its first run found:

- **the tenth alike name ended the extraction.** `BumpName` numbered
  `~1`..`~9` and then returned -1, which the engine reads as *abort the
  archive*. Live since M10; 26 entries produced 10 files (BLOCKERS.md). Now
  `~99`, and an unplaceable name fails **its own entry** — the allocation
  rule applied to names.
- **the mock Toolbox never refused anything.** `PBDirCreateSync` tolerated
  `EEXIST`; `PBGetCatInfoSync` returned `noErr` over an untouched block. So
  `EnsureDir`'s dupFNErr branch had never run under test, and the
  folder-collision case passing since 2026-08-28 passed for the wrong reason.

Neither was reachable by the corpus (932 fixtures, no two names alike for 31
characters, nothing damaged) or the mock. **An archive built to make the
interface say every sentence it has** is a different instrument from a
fixture built to be decoded.


## 2026-08-29 (a cut archive) — where the archive ends and where the file ends

Checked rather than asserted: every entry the engine declines reaches the
sink. What does not is an entry the walk never reaches, and three formats
ended walks wrongly:

- **DiskDoubler DDAR** has no end marker, so an unreadable header was taken
  for the end and a cut download reported success. The end is now the file's
  end exactly; arriving short of or past it is truncation, and every position
  inside must hold a `DDAR` magic.
- **DiskDoubler DDA2 never checked its end marker.** Leaving the loop any
  other way is now `UNC_ERR_TRUNCATED` — except running out INSIDE the file
  with less than a record left, which the corpus showed is a real ending
  (`derived-DD_Expand.sea`: 38 bytes, no marker, `unar` reads it; the first
  rule failed `./ci.sh` 931/932). Being sent PAST the end is a cut. A cut
  inside that 46-byte window is indistinguishable and documented as such
  (TESTING.md).
- **StuffIt clamps the stated length to the file's**, which erased the
  evidence. It clamps and REMEMBERS now; a walk finished under a clamp returns
  truncated.

**A walk's end condition has to distinguish "the archive said it was over"
from "the bytes ran out".** Wherever the two were one branch, a cut file
became a complete run.

### The suite that could not have caught it, and the one that does

`run_robustness.py` has truncated every fixture at four fractions since M2
and requires "a normal exit code" — exit 0 is one — so it passed 9,320
variants over both defects (BLOCKERS.md's tenth smell). `tools/run_truncation.py`
asks the oracle: where `unar` calls a cut archive broken, so must we. It found
the StuffIt defect the hand scan had missed **because the hand scan picked
fixtures alphabetically** (for DiskDoubler, two single-file archives). The
suite was written with the same bug, passed against a deliberately broken
build, and now chooses the most-entried fixtures.

## 2026-08-29 (two MIME gaps) — the item described our own binary, and nobody had run it

OPEN_ITEMS.md's *"Waiting on a file this machine does not have"* carried two
MIME entries from M36 making four statements; three were false, each one
command from being checked.

**`x-uuencode` inside a multipart** — *"mpack decodes those; this does not"*:
both halves wrong. munpack's encodings are `enc_none, enc_qp, enc_base64`
(`reference/mpack/decode.c`); an unknown encoding falls through as
`enc_none`, `handleUuencode` is reached only for a depth-0 `text/*` part with
no encoding, `filename` or `name`, so munpack writes the uuencoded TEXT. This
engine always decoded it (the uu probe wins the sniff), 36 bytes byte-exact.
The real defect was unstated: a uu part shadows the MIME walk, so a two-part
message lists `uupart.txt` alone where munpack also writes `wanted.bin`.

**`message/partial`** — the "missing" specimen is written by
`mpack -m 10000 -o out.mime payload.bin` (30,000 bytes into four parts), and
munpack reassembles them byte-exact, given two things: it reassembles through
`/usr/tmp/m-prts-$USER`, which it does not create; and it creates `CT` with
`O_EXCL`, so parts 2..n die with *"CT: File exists"* unless `CT` is removed
between invocations. The entry also said this engine decodes "each file on
its own"; none of the four parts decodes at all, and `src/fmt_mime.c` did not
contain the word *partial*.

**What transfers** (now in BLOCKERS.md's list): **an open item that describes
what our own binary does is the cheapest claim to check, and the one most
likely to have been written rather than run.** *Waiting on a file* is a
decision to stop looking; neither item was blocked on a file.

## 2026-08-29 (a Macintosh wrote a MIME message) — the port was in the reference tree

`src/fmt_mime.c` is transcribed from mpack 1.6 and had only been graded on
Linux-made messages; the gap was an `application/applefile` part a MACINTOSH
wrote. The entry named "mpack's own Macintosh port" — which is in
`reference/mpack`, the tree `tools/build_mpack.sh` had built munpack from
since M36. `tools/macmime/` compiles `encode_applefile()` and `encode()`
unmodified for a 68000 with host glue; `tools/vmac/macmime.py` runs it on
System 6.0.8. The message is 1,912 bytes and passes 18/18, both forks
byte-exact through this engine and readable by munpack.

**What is mpack's and what is ours.** Every byte-deciding file is mpack's
(encode.c, macfile.c, codes.c, magic.c, md5c.c, xmalloc.c); ours is Toolbox
glue and two `os_` entry points. Line endings are the C library's, so this
specimen cannot settle them (FORMATS.md).

### Retro68's newlib cannot open a file on System 6.0.8

The stdio build hung silently: a bare
`open("Probe1.tmp", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666)` **never returns**
(photographed at 40 s and 80 s).

**This is a symptom and not an attribution.** Retro68's `_open_r`
(`libretro/syscalls.c`) does `HCreate(0,0,…)`, `HOpenDF(0,0,…)`, then `HOpen`
on `paramErr`; which hangs has not been reduced to a reproduction, so it is
not a finding. `HOpenDF`'s `paramErr` is documented behaviour, and zeroing the
stack before `open()` does not change the hang (2026-10-13, *the bug was the
footnote*).

The fix needs none of that: newlib's `funopen()` builds a `FILE *` from four
callbacks over the same fully-zeroed HFS param blocks the application uses,
reading the LIVE forks as macos.c's `Macopen()` did. The engine's "no libc"
rule had bought the application the same immunity.

### A harness that could not put a Finder flag on the volume

One check of eighteen failed: Finder flags `0x0000` where the subject was
built with `0x0100`. **`hcopy -m` does not carry the Finder flags** (a
MacBinary with byte 73 `0x01` round-trips as `0x00`). They are now set on the
Mac with `PBHSetFInfoSync` and the catalogue re-read before mpack sees the
file. **A fixture is not what you built, it is what arrived.**

### The subject has to be in the blessed folder

`mkboot.py` puts the shell application in the System Folder, whose directory
is the default; a subject at the volume root gave `PBGetCatInfo` −43. Two
runs; the on-screen progress said so the first time.

### What it does not do

One message from one encoder. Eudora 1.2 (in the corpus) and Claris Emailer
(not) have not been run; that is a different specimen, not an open item.

## 2026-08-29 (a part that hid its message) — the strongest scan is not the strongest claim

`unc_sniff` runs the uuencode, btoa and BinHex probes before MIME, which is
right for a posting whose body is one document and wrong for a multipart:
those probes scan ANYWHERE, so a uu part plus a base64 attachment was claimed
whole by the uu walk (`macextract l` listed `uupart.txt` alone; previous
entry).

**What changed.** `unc_mime_probe_multipart` — refusing anything without a
`multipart/*` WITH a boundary — runs before those three. A `.hqx` or `.uu`
posting still belongs to its format; asserted both ways in
`tools/run_mime.py`.

**Not losing a capability.** mpack drops a `text/*` part with no filename as
the sender's note (`handleMessage`), so the walk now applies `handleUuencode()`'s
body test at every depth (`mime_body_nested()`). A uu part decodes through
`fmt_uu.c`'s helpers — exported, not transcribed twice — named from its
`begin` line. `Content-Transfer-Encoding: x-uuencode` does not decide (mpack
has no such value); the body does.

**A BinHex or btoa document in that position is kept as it lies**, named
`partN`, rather than dropped; `macextract` handles it when handed back.

**What transfers.** The probe order was documented as CONFIDENCE, and a scan
finding a document is strong evidence that one is there — and none about what
ELSE is there. **Ask what a probe's evidence bounds, not just how strong it
is**: a marker found by scanning bounds a region, never a file.

## 2026-08-29 (a message in several files) — the sixth join scheme, and the first whose parts are text

`message/partial` (RFC 2046 5.2.2) was the last of OPEN_ITEMS.md's *"not
written, and not waiting for anything"*; mpack `-m` and munpack were the
oracle.

**A join scheme, not a shape of the MIME reader**: the parts are FILES and
the engine never opens a file. Part 1's body begins with the enclosed
message's headers, so the concatenation IS a message and the reader is
`unc_mime_extract` — no intermediate file. (mpack composes enclosing plus
inner headers because its result is read by a person; ours is parsed.)

**Two properties no other scheme has**, each a change to the joiner:

- **Every part's header is a different length.** `UncSegmentDesc.head_len` is
  one per set; the joiner now asks a per-part `hdr` hook, keeps the answer for
  the OPEN part only (`SegJoin.curhdr`), and the hook re-proves `number` and
  `id` — the structural check in place of a fingerprint.
- **The set declares a part COUNT and no byte total.** An UNKNOWN `total` ran
  the flat walk off the map and reported an ended set as missing a part; the
  joiner learns the total when it opens the last part.

**Identity by content, through a different call.** The `id` parameter is
content, but `unc_segment_match` gets 100 bytes and mail headers are longer,
so both hosts use `unc_segment_describe`. Only the LAST part carries `total`,
so a set opened elsewhere asks for its count as Compact Pro asks for its
index segment — the Mac shell's `SegFindLast` answers both.

**What the oracle cost**: munpack's directory and `CT` quirks (previous
entry), in `tools/run_mime.py` and TESTING.md; an exit-status-only harness
would have read them as our defects.

**It joined on a Mac Plus the same day**, at 4 MB and the 1 MB floor, as a
case in `tools/vmac/segcheck.py`, checked on the Out volume (four TEXT files
becoming one file with a resource fork), not the on-screen grid.

**Stack.** The only chain through the engine twice (joiner → reader → joiner),
so measured: 2,796 B on a 68000, second to DiskDoubler's 3,386 B, against a
4 KB rule (FORMATS.md, *Stack*).

## 2026-08-29 (the chain that was walked twice) — the postfix byte was the last one the walk wrote

Profiling `derived-EmpireBuilderDemo.sit` (the archive Expander unstuffs in
three quarters of our time; FORMATS.md, *Timed on the same Mac Plus*) found
two things.

**The fixture has no method 13 in it.** Its forks are methods 2 and 3; the
profile is 58 % `unc_lzw_read`, 26 % `unc_huff_decode`, 7.7 %
`unc_crc16_arc`. FORMATS.md's decode-cost row said "StuffIt (13)" and reasoned
from the label while `unc_huff_decode`'s comment called it a method-3 run.
**The file nobody was reading was right**; corrected in place.

**LZW walked every symbol's parents twice.** `lzw_firstbyte` walked the chain
for the postfix byte, then the expansion walked it again. The chain is written
reversed, so the postfix is `chain[n-1]`, free. It survived M29 because it
transcribes `LZW.c`'s `NextLZWSymbol`, where the walks sit in different
functions; a profile attributes cost to functions, not to the order of steps
inside one. **A duplicated walk reads as one walk each in every measurement
that attributes cost to functions.**

- **KwKwK costs a slot, not a walk**: the previous chain goes one slot up and
  `chain[0]` takes the root.
- **`lzw_grow` moved before the walk**, since it reallocates and resets the
  chain; nothing between reads what it moves.
- **Both hot loops now use locals** instead of `z->parent`, `z->chr`,
  `z->capsymbols`, `z->chainpos`, `produced` per byte — worth more than the
  walk on this corpus's short chains (2.9 bytes a code on the StuffIt fixture).

**Measured**: −16.3 % on `popper-1.7.tar.Z` down to −1.4 % on
`synth-arc-mixed.arc`, and **0.00 % — identical instruction counts** — on six
fixtures that never reach this decoder (FORMATS.md, *Decode cost*). Heap
unmoved. **The branch is graded**: a counter build over all 946 fixtures takes
the KwKwK path in **111** (`.Z`, DiskDoubler method 1, StuffIt method 2), so
it is inside the differential suite.

## 2026-08-30 (the flush that was not the answer) — a screen cannot see a commit

Hypothesis tested: *"Expander's 56 s and our 76 s do not cover the same
work"* — our sink flushes per fork, Expander's output reaches the volume only
when it quits. **It is real, under a second, and explains none of the gap.**

**The first instrument measured nothing and said "3 s".** Timing Command-Q by
screenshot hit the poll floor for both applications and a 1.6 KB control,
because Expander's frames either side are **byte-identical**. **An instrument
that can only see repaints reports the floor for everything that does not
repaint, and the floor looks like a small number rather than a missing one.**

**The image is the instrument.** A copy of `boot.hfv` mounted mid-run, read at
the last changed frame, after the quit key and after the kill: our three files
are there when the clock stops; Expander's four appear within a second of the
keystroke. On this emulator a commit is a host `memcpy`; a real Mac Plus
writing 415 KB would not pay zero, which is a MANUAL_TESTS.md question.

The same probe corrected a wrong inference: identical frames had read as
"Command-Q did not quit". **Two explanations fit "the screen did not change" —
nothing happened, and something happened invisibly — and only a second
instrument tells them apart.**

**What is left**: 57 s against our 73 s with both outputs on disk, so decode
and I/O — 58 % `unc_lzw_read`, 26 % `unc_huff_decode`, 8 % `unc_crc16_arc`,
the last being the 2-3x table twice declined at 3 KB of code (2026-08-27,
*what the tables left behind*).
